   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem.

Usage:
- This tool will overwrite the existing file if there is one at the provided path.
- If this is an existing file outside the working directory, you MUST use the Read tool first to read the file's contents. This tool will fail if you did not.

Deliver your final report to the agent that spawned you (your caller). Use it once, for that hand-off only: when your work is complete, call SubagentHandback({message: <your full report>}) as your last tool call and then stop. It is not a messaging channel: do not use it for progress updates or questions.

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Firecrawl provides web, developer, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. For a biomedical, life-science, clinical, or arXiv literature question, the firecrawl_research_* tools search the paper index, while categories: ["research"] on firecrawl_search filters ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites. Use the firecrawl_research_* tools to search academic and research literature, expand from anchor papers via the citation graph, and read full-text passages from a specific paper. ## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.
- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.
- First navigation for a task is `new_tab(url)`, not `goto_url(url)`. The daemon
  preserves the attached tab across separate CLI invocations, so do not call

## Testing and assessment

- Assessment is continuous, not a single test day: start with movement quality, injury history, and training background, then observe daily via warm-ups and practice. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5]
- Testing protocol has to be exactly repeatable over time ("how you do it in January needs to be the same as how you do it in April") or the resulting data cannot be trusted for comparison. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.6]
- Favor a small number of valid, reliable tests mapped to clear KPI categories over an exhaustive battery — illustrated with a simple baseball profile (bodyweight, 60-yard dash, vertical jump, broad jump, back squat, push-up max). **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.6; week1-lecture.md p.16]
- Weekly tracking is preferred over infrequent (e.g., once-a-phase) testing, specifically to catch plateaus or declines early enough to adjust programming. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.7]
- Preparedness (the athlete's underlying physical capability, built over a long period) is explicitly distinguished from readiness (day-to-day fluctuation) — both are tracked, but they answer different questions. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.7]
- Reassessment timing is governed by three factors: proximity to competition, the expected magnitude of change for that training phase and athlete level, and current recovery status — "do not reassess an athlete if there is known fatigue." **Inferred (author uncertain)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md, "Reassessment"]
- 1RM testing is reserved for intermediate/advanced athletes with real exposure to near-maximal loads; novices and most women's-sport testing default to repetition-max protocols, which are described as better tolerated neurologically, psychologically, and physically for smaller-framed lifters. **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.18; week1-lecture.md p.39]
- Velocity-based 1RM estimation (linear-displacement transducer, ~10% load increments to 85-90% or a target mean velocity) is preferred over live 1RM attempts to avoid the fatigue and injury risk of true maxing, with published target mean velocities at 1RM (squat 0.3 m/s, bench 0.2 m/s, power hang snatch 1.0 m/s, power hang clean 0.8 m/s). **Inferred (author uncertain — legacy protocol, see Tensions)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md]
- The Baylor Sport Assessment Table (V4) assigns a specific battery per sport (movement screen, anthropometrics, CMJ, broad jump, weighted throw, upper/lower strength estimation, strength endurance, aerobic fitness, repeat sprint ability, linear sprint, change of direction) rather than testing every sport the same way. **Inferred** [update-baylor-sport-assessment-table-v4.md]
- The current data dictionary is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch, ForceDecks, Polar), not by sport, which Eric's own gap analysis flags as a real usability problem for staff and a priority to fix with sport-specific, threshold-contextualized dictionaries. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2]

## Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring

- Force plates (CMJ testing) were already the department's longitudinal performance-tracking tool well before the 2022-23 wellness-survey experiment, and remained in place after that experiment ended. **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
- Modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker in place of subjective wellness questionnaires, because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys never quite were." **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
- The standard CMJ family run on ForceDecks: hands-free squat, squat jump (quarter-squat start, 3s hold), countermovement jump (x3), hop test / repeated CMJ (10 reps total, n=5 pairs), and single-leg CMJ (x3 per leg) — each with a scripted weigh-in, stabilization, and rep protocol. **Inferred (protocol; author uncertain)** [revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md]
- The isometric seated calf raise is run on the ForceDecks "Mid-Thigh Pull" setting: 90-degree ankle/knee position, belt pre-tensioned to a fingertip's gap, 3 maximal 6-second contractions with 15 seconds' rest between reps. **Inferred (protocol)** [protocol-iso-seated-calf-raise.md; revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md]
- Metric selection for force-plate reporting follows a disciplined framework: pick 1-2 output metrics (the obvious performance result, e.g. jump height), 1-3 driver metrics (what produces the output, e.g. braking/propulsive force), 1-3 strategy metrics (how the athlete achieved it, e.g. phase durations), optional symmetry metrics (L/R differences), and add "fluffy" metrics (peak power, average power, RFD) only with a specific, defensible rationale. **Adopted practice, framework not Eric's own** [hd-odsf-metrics.md — origin: Hawkin Dynamics]
- NordBord hamstring testing was retired for roster-wide football monitoring (after starting January 2023) because a 25-30 minute per-group session could not be sustained across 120+ athletes without large, uncontrolled gaps in the data, and staff turnover ended the coordination needed to run it at scale. The decision rule stated: keep a demanding test only where you have "smaller numbers, clear clinical purpose, dedicated oversight" (now used for targeted return-to-play groups paired with joint-specific isometric testing); drop it where you can't guarantee consistent, comparable collection. **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]

## Load monitoring and GPS

- The core GPS technology stack is Catapult (device/OpenField software) with Kitman Labs as the central athlete-management system for cross-technology storage, scaling, and visualization. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7]
- Core GPS metrics tracked: maximum velocity, total distance, player load, field time, heart-rate bands, velocity/acceleration/deceleration effort bands, and Inertial Movement Analysis (IMA) for indoor sessions without GPS coverage. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.11-13, Data Dictionary]
- A documented step-by-step SOP exists for the full GPS session lifecycle: charging, alarm-setting, activity creation, live period management, post-session sync, data cleaning (spike detection), tagging, and PDF export/reporting. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.9-11]
- No sport-specific or position-specific GPS/load thresholds currently exist in the documented data dictionary — it is generic and vendor-organized, and building contextualized per-sport thresholds is named as unfinished, prioritized work. **Explicit (gap, stated as a gap)** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2]
- Heavy GPS/load-monitoring data was described as having bred a "culture of fear" in the field broadly (do less, to protect recovery), which the course material argues actually leaves athletes under-prepared for competition. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10]
- Daily subjective wellness surveys, rolled out across multiple sports via the AMS app starting summer 2022, were abandoned after roughly one academic year because athletes learned to game the consistent, low-effort answers the survey rewarded; the data looked clean but carried no real signal. Wellness surveys are still used, deliberately, in return-to-play scenarios and with athletes managing chronic health conditions, where subjective context still adds value objective data can't supply. **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]

## Speed and sprint

- Linear sprint testing uses a 2-point start for team-sport athletes (for reliability), athlete self-selected start timing, at least two maximal-effort reps over 30-40 meters. **Inferred (author uncertain)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md]
- Split times are interpreted by physical quality, not just total time: 0-10m is read as an acceleration score (reflecting maximal strength/power/slow stretch-shortening-cycle development), 30-40m as a speed score (reflecting sprint-specific/fast stretch-shortening-cycle development), and 40m peak velocity is derived from the 30-40m split divided by 10. **Inferred (author uncertain)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md]
- SmartSpeed timing gates are the standard tool for sprint, agility, and reaction-time testing across the department. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7]
- Speed is taught as the quality with the shortest ground-contact-time demand (~0.08s male, ~0.10s female at max velocity) and is described as harder to train and more genetically constrained than strength or power, but as the biggest separator between good and great athletes at the elite level. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.11]

## Strength and power

- The Vermeil hierarchy of athletic development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill, each level a required foundation for the next) is repeatedly described as the department's programming "compass." **Inferred (transcript + shared course material)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10; week1-lecture.md pp.23,26]
- Exercise selection is organized on a spectrum from general preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises (Bondarchuk), replacing the loose and often-misapplied idea of "sport specific." **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16; week1-lecture.md pp.32-36]
- The Principle of Dynamic Correspondence (Verkhoshansky) — matching amplitude/direction of movement, region of force production, dynamics of effort, rate/timing of force production, and regime of muscular work to the sport skill — governs whether an exercise actually transfers, rather than surface resemblance to the sport. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.14; week1-lecture.md p.34]
- Training time is deliberately weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints); single-joint assistance work is kept to a small share of total volume. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.13; week1-lecture.md p.31]
- Off-season strength work prioritizes relative strength and technique first; already-strong athletes shift more time toward strength-speed/speed-strength work. In-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than trying to build strength while managing a full competition schedule. **Inferred (transcript + shared slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21; hhpr-5355-class-8-2026.md p.21]
- Undulating/non-linear periodization (Parker/Miller/Panariello), waving volume week to week (e.g., medium-high, medium, high, low over four weeks) is stated as the personally preferred model over strict linear progression, specifically to avoid staleness while still building tolerance for higher loads. **Inferred (transcript, speaker unconfirmed but first-person: "For me personally, this is a more preferential model to use")** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-26]
- Prilepin's chart (total reps and reps-per-set by %1RM) is the default guide for daily rep/set assignment within a training block, used consistently across strength and power teaching. **Inferred/Explicit (shared team material)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.19; hhpr-5355-class-8-2026.md p.15]
- Strength's residual training effect is treated as roughly 30 days — a minimal retention dose is still trained within that window, even during lower-strength-emphasis blocks. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-25]
- Tracy Fober's maxim ("use a barbell like a chisel, not a sledgehammer") is adopted as a guiding standard: prioritize movement quality and confidence-through-competence over chasing hypertrophy or 1RM numbers, especially early in a training cycle. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.21; week1-lecture.md p.46]

## Conditioning and energy systems

- Conditioning is defined two ways: (1) how well an athlete can meet the energy requirements of their specific sport/activity, and (2) how well they sustain strength, speed, and power output across a full competition. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.22]
- All three energy systems (alactic ~10-12s highest power, glycolytic/anaerobic-lactic ~60-90s medium capacity, aerobic hours-long lowest power/highest capacity) are always active simultaneously; programming targets the adaptation, not the drill label. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.19; class-4-2026.md p.15]
- A sport cannot maximize all three energy systems at once — priority has to be picked based on what the competition actually demands (e.g., for football: prepared for fall camp first, then the first game). **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.31]
- For football specifically, the stated priority stack is: Goal 1, alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp demands; Goal 2, the same two systems for game demands; glycolytic conditioning is treated as a "worst case scenario" to be absorbed incidentally through camp and practice rather than programmed as a primary target. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md pp.34, 39]
- Anaerobic (lactate) threshold heart-rate zones are assigned by athlete body size rather than a single number: roughly 165 bpm for big/tall athletes, 170 for medium, 175 for small, with Zone 1-4 bands set as percentages of that individual threshold. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md pp.28-29]
- The traits easiest to build (aerobic) are lost fastest under detraining; the traits hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest — this ordering is used to sequence what needs the most frequent re-exposure. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.47]
- Training intensities between roughly 75-90% of maximal effort are labeled (via Francis) "no man's land" — too fast to build alactic power cleanly, too slow to build real aerobic capacity — and are treated as a zone to generally avoid as a primary training target. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.48]
- "Everything we do is some form of conditioning": lifting, agility work, and skill drills each load a specific energy system (power vs. capacity, alactic/glycolytic/aerobic) and should be classified and counted as conditioning, not treated as separate from it. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.31, tables pp.35-42]
- For speed-power athletes, the aerobic system's main value is inter-effort recovery (regenerating ATP between bouts), not distance capacity — a better-developed aerobic system means more available energy on play 10, 11, or 12 of a drive, not longer continuous running ability. **Inferred (transcript)** [2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md p.9]
- Aerobic-system training is kept below anaerobic threshold with roughly a 1:1 to 1:2 work:rest ratio and a general speed ceiling around 4.5 m/s, specifically to avoid spilling over into glycolytic-system stress. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.51; 2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.11-12]
- Joel Jamieson's *Ultimate MMA Conditioning* is recommended as the single best practical resource for energy-system development, on the basis that its methods transfer cleanly to non-combat sports despite the MMA framing. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md pp.49-50; 2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.11-12]

## Rehab and return to play

- Applied Performance's stated role in return-to-performance is to supply information that supports Athletics Performance and Athletic Medicine's decisions on training and RTP periodization — a support/advisory role, not a stated final-decision role. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
- KPI-threshold identification for diagnostic screening and performance testing is named as a departmental operating principle, but no specific RTP criteria, battery, or phased-return protocol appears anywhere in this corpus. **Explicit (principle) / gap (no criteria stated)** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
- Daily wellness-style subjective monitoring, dropped for general roster use, is explicitly kept in return-to-play scenarios specifically because subjective context still fills a gap objective testing can't. **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
- NordBord hamstring testing, dropped for roster-wide use, is explicitly retained for smaller, targeted return-to-play groups paired with joint-specific isometric testing (ForceFrame-style). **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]

*This is the thinnest discipline in the corpus — see Interview prep.*

## Injury risk and prevention

- Injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, through sound progression of load, training means, and density, in collaboration with Athletic Medicine — an explicit refusal to claim injury prevention as achievable. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.4; week1-lecture.md p.9]
- Bodyweight-control competency is treated as a marker of injury risk in its own right: an athlete who can bench 400 lb but can't do 10 clean push-ups has "something out of whack" that needs fixing regardless of their strength numbers. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5]
- Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design; abrupt, large changes are treated as a direct injury-risk driver, not just a training-quality issue. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.27]
- No formal injury-risk model (ACWR, tissue-capacity tracking, a biomechanical screening protocol with defined red flags) is attributed to Eric anywhere in this corpus; the detailed treatment of ACWR and injury-risk modeling that does exist (Clemson curriculum) is reference material only, not confirmed Baylor practice.

## Recovery and sleep

- Recovery capacity must be "earned" by training hard enough first; recovery technology (Theragun, Normatec, cryo) is treated as useful but not a substitute for managing training stress and dose correctly. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.9]
- Recovery appears in the department's own subcategory list of Athletic Performance (alongside strength, conditioning, speed, agility, power, nutrition, applied performance, sports psychology, RTP), but no specific recovery protocol, sleep target, or monitoring tool is described anywhere in this corpus. **Explicit (named as a subcategory) / gap (no protocol stated)** [week1-lecture.md p.11]

## Nutrition and body composition

- Performance Nutrition is explicitly a separate Health & Wellness unit from Applied Performance, owning individual nutrition consultations, supplement education, body composition and bone density assessment, and the training table/fueling stations. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.5]
- Body composition testing is capped at no more than 4 times per year. **Inferred (author uncertain)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md, "Anthropometrics"]
- Anthropometrics (height, weight, muscle-to-fat ratio) are described as strongly associated with success in most sports and worth tracking even though they are owned by Performance Nutrition rather than Applied Performance. **Inferred (author uncertain)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md, "Anthropometrics"]
- No nutrition decision rules, body-composition targets, or thresholds are attributed to Eric anywhere in this corpus; this appears to be a deliberate department-design choice (Performance Nutrition owns it) rather than an oversight.

## Coaching, skill acquisition and constraints-led approach

- A trained "coach's eye," built through repetition and attention, is treated as at least as important as any technology for daily assessment: "you don't need a fancy test or anything to do that. But you do have to have a good coach's eye." **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.8]
- New movement patterns are expected to take roughly 3-4 weeks of practice to become efficient and low-energy-cost, which informs how much proficiency to expect when a new exercise or drill is introduced. **Inferred (transcript)** [2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.6-7]
- Movement efficiency (skill) is treated as directly reducing energy cost — elite athletes (cited examples: LeBron James, Deion Sanders) are described as outlasting and outperforming peers partly through tactical efficiency that lowers the physical output required to achieve the same result. **Inferred (transcript)** [2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.8-9]
- Basic movement skills and basic lifts are taught before anything advanced, on the observed premise that many incoming athletes have high sport-specific skill from early specialization but poor general movement competency. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5]

*Relatively thin as an independently-stated coaching philosophy in Eric's own voice specifically — most of this section is shared course/team material; see Interview prep.*

1	# Review and Plan: Fundamentals of On-Field Rehabilitation (Sportsmith)
2	
3	Eric Rash, Director of Applied Performance, Baylor Athletics
4	Written 2026-09-25. Private working document.
5	
6	Source: Simon Harries, *The Fundamentals of On-Field Rehabilitation* (Sportsmith). Seven parts: seven PDFs plus seven videos, about 2 h 10 min in total. Every PDF and every transcript in this folder was read. The transcripts are machine speech-to-text checked against the player captions; nobody listened back to the audio. Two terms are still unclear, Part 3 at about 15:51 and Part 6 at about 02:24. They are left unclear here too.
7	
8	## 1. What the course is
9	
10	It is one AFL practitioner's framework for the bridge from gym to field. It has three parts:
11	
12	- **Five levels.** Level 1 to Level 5, then a return to training.
13	- **Three pillars.** Linear running from submaximal to maximal velocity (MV), multidirectional speed and agility, and sport-specific skill.
14	- **Two axes.** Intensity (competency, then capacity) and complexity (control, then chaos).
15	
16	The course ends with a four-step recipe for building your own framework: levels, pillars, intensity factors, drill menu.
17	
18	The numbers that make it worth owning come from the Part 3 transcript, because the PDF lost the table:
19	
20	| Level | Target % of max velocity | Typical content |
21	|---|---|---|
22	| 1 | 50–70% | Running prep drills (dribbles, A-skips, pogos, scissors); fixed-distance repeats with a time target (60 m in 13 → 12 → 11 s) |
23	| 2 | 70–75% | Faster 60 m repeats; COD under 45° |
24	| 3 | 75–85% | Broken strides: 20 m accelerate, 20 m hold, 20 m decelerate, with only the hold phase timed (e.g. 2.88–3.0 s ≈ 24–25 km/h); closed-reactive drills |
25	| 4 | 85–95% | Undulating sessions; flies; open-reactive drills; bigger spaces |
26	| 5 | >95–100% | Evasive and competitive work; repeat sprints (2 × 3–4 × 40 m, all >85% MV, one every 30 s) |
27	
28	**The gate at 75–85% MV.** Before a player runs faster than this, the course checks four things:
29	- enough healing time;
30	- earlier sessions came back with minimal pain or awareness of the area;
31	- force benchmarks: Nordic at least 80–85% of the player's pre-injury value for hamstrings, seated calf isometric about 1.7–1.8× body weight for the calf;
32	- a reactive-strength hop test.
33	
34	**The exit rule.** At least one, ideally two, exposures above 90% MV before return. He gives no fixed number and says it depends on context.
35	
36	## 2. Objective opinion
37	
38	**Verdict: worth keeping as a dosage reference. It is weak as a teaching model and not built for football. Take the numbers, not the theory.**
39	
40	What is strong:
41	
42	1. **Session-level numbers are rare, and this course has them.** The 60 m timed repeats, the broken-stride timing, the linear-then-undulating shift at about 80–85%, the 75–85% gate, and the repeat-sprint format can all be written into a plan tomorrow. Most RTP writing stops at "progress gradually."
43	2. **The intensity levers are the most useful single table in the course.** For multidirectional work he names eight dials: velocity change, entry velocity, COD angle, preparation distance or time, space, reactivity, % effort, and % MV. He also points out that they interact: shrinking the space caps the entry speed. That gives you a checklist, not a feel.
44	3. **Intensity and complexity are separate axes.** He is explicit that a new level does not make every drill chaotic. Some actions stay controlled at high intensity while others are already in chaos. That is correct, and many practitioners get it wrong.
45	4. **The case studies are honest.**
46	   - Case 1 returned without ever exceeding 90% MV.
47	   - Case 2 returned a week before the staff recommendation.
48	   - Sprint volume was under-dosed at 40% of game value.
49	   - A low high-speed-running threshold (17 km/h) twice inflated the totals by accident.
50	
51	   Real practice looks like this, and it shows where the framework bends.
52	
53	What is weak:
54	
55	1. **It is Matt Taberner's control-chaos continuum with a velocity layer added.** Harries credits Taberner himself. You already hold five Taberner papers (see `RTP_Constraints_Course/RESOURCES.md`). The course adds nothing new to the theory; its new value is the worked numbers.
56	2. **The complexity axis rests on older motor-learning theory, not ecological dynamics.** This matters most for Joe's course.
57	   - Blocked → serial → random practice is contextual interference, from the Schmidt information-processing tradition.
58	   - His "closed reactivity" example is a coach throwing a hand signal. That is a generic stimulus, not the information a player actually uses in a game, such as a defender's hips.
59	   - He mentions "constraints-based learning design" once, in Part 2, in one sentence, and never puts it into practice.
60	   - In this model, complexity is something added once intensity is safe. In an ecological model, the right information has to be present from the start and scaled, not switched on at Level 4.
61	3. **The progression criteria are almost all physical.** Healing time, pain, force benchmarks and % MV are all measured. The one behavioural criterion ("if they hesitate… they are not ready") is stated in Part 2 and never measured. That hesitation is exactly the subjective judgement Joe says he cannot defend to objective people.
62	4. **AFL is not American football.** AFL is continuous: about 13 km a game and about 200 m of very-high-speed running. Football is intermittent, position-specific and built around collision. The % MV logic transfers; the thresholds do not.
63	   - The 17/23/27 km/h bands and "% of game value" have to be re-derived for each position from Baylor GPS.
64	   - Many linemen may rarely or never reach a 27 km/h sprint threshold in a game. Check that in our data before assuming it either way.
65	5. **Contact is missing as a pillar.** Tackling appears once, as a word. For football, collision and contact (block, shed, tackle, hand-fight, stance start) is a fourth pillar. It is also where Joe's "I am not the right constraint" case sits: the lineman who needed real bodies.
66	6. **Evidence quality.** The benchmarks (80–85% Nordic, 1.8× body weight calf isometric, two exposures above 90%) are expert opinion and common practice, not results from trials. He says so himself ("varied opinions in the field"). Label them that way whenever they are used.
67	7. **He deliberately de-emphasised GPS** so the framework would work without it. Your job is GPS, so for you that is the part to reverse, not copy.
68	
69	## 3. How it helps you understand the concepts
70	
71	| Concept in the course | What you already have | The gap it fills for you |
72	|---|---|---|
73	| % MV bands per level | Each player's MV and speed zones in the Catapult pipeline | An agreed, measurable language with Athletic Medicine: "Level 3 means 75–85% of *his* MV" |
74	| 75–85% gate | Force plate and Nordic data (ForceDecks, NordBord) | A **decision gate** you can compute. This is Old Bull Lab 2D in practice, and it separates monitoring (a GPS trend) from testing (a gate check), which is Lab 2C |
75	| Linear → undulating | You already undulate load across the team week | The same logic applied to one returning player, anchored to the team's Tue/Wed high, Thu low pattern. Joe asked for this in his tool spec |
76	| High-speed / very-high-speed / sprint volume as % of game value | Game demands by position | A running "% of game" line per player that Joe can see, for example 40% (under-dosed) vs 70–80% (on track) |
77	| Eight intensity levers | Nothing formal | A shared checklist for why a drill is harder, and the input schema for Joe's drill-design tool |

# Review and Plan: Fundamentals of On-Field Rehabilitation (Sportsmith)

Eric Rash, Director of Applied Performance, Baylor Athletics
Written 2026-09-25. Private working document.

Source: Simon Harries, *The Fundamentals of On-Field Rehabilitation* (Sportsmith). Seven parts: seven PDFs plus seven videos, about 2 h 10 min in total. Every PDF and every transcript in this folder was read. The transcripts are machine speech-to-text checked against the player captions; nobody listened back to the audio. Two terms are still unclear, Part 3 at about 15:51 and Part 6 at about 02:24. They are left unclear here too.

## 1. What the course is

It is one AFL practitioner's framework for the bridge from gym to field. It has three parts:

- **Five levels.** Level 1 to Level 5, then a return to training.
- **Three pillars.** Linear running from submaximal to maximal velocity (MV), multidirectional speed and agility, and sport-specific skill.
- **Two axes.** Intensity (competency, then capacity) and complexity (control, then chaos).

The course ends with a four-step recipe for building your own framework: levels, pillars, intensity factors, drill menu.

The numbers that make it worth owning come from the Part 3 transcript, because the PDF lost the table:

| Level | Target % of max velocity | Typical content |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 50–70% | Running prep drills (dribbles, A-skips, pogos, scissors); fixed-distance repeats with a time target (60 m in 13 → 12 → 11 s) |
| 2 | 70–75% | Faster 60 m repeats; COD under 45° |
| 3 | 75–85% | Broken strides: 20 m accelerate, 20 m hold, 20 m decelerate, with only the hold phase timed (e.g. 2.88–3.0 s ≈ 24–25 km/h); closed-reactive drills |
| 4 | 85–95% | Undulating sessions; flies; open-reactive drills; bigger spaces |
| 5 | >95–100% | Evasive and competitive work; repeat sprints (2 × 3–4 × 40 m, all >85% MV, one every 30 s) |

**The gate at 75–85% MV.** Before a player runs faster than this, the course checks four things:
- enough healing time;
- earlier sessions came back with minimal pain or awareness of the area;
- force benchmarks: Nordic at least 80–85% of the player's pre-injury value for hamstrings, seated calf isometric about 1.7–1.8× body weight for the calf;
- a reactive-strength hop test.

**The exit rule.** At least one, ideally two, exposures above 90% MV before return. He gives no fixed number and says it depends on context.

## 2. Objective opinion

**Verdict: worth keeping as a dosage reference. It is weak as a teaching model and not built for football. Take the numbers, not the theory.**

What is strong:

1. **Session-level numbers are rare, and this course has them.** The 60 m timed repeats, the broken-stride timing, the linear-then-undulating shift at about 80–85%, the 75–85% gate, and the repeat-sprint format can all be written into a plan tomorrow. Most RTP writing stops at "progress gradually."
2. **The intensity levers are the most useful single table in the course.** For multidirectional work he names eight dials: velocity change, entry velocity, COD angle, preparation distance or time, space, reactivity, % effort, and % MV. He also points out that they interact: shrinking the space caps the entry speed. That gives you a checklist, not a feel.
3. **Intensity and complexity are separate axes.** He is explicit that a new level does not make every drill chaotic. Some actions stay controlled at high intensity while others are already in chaos. That is correct, and many practitioners get it wrong.
4. **The case studies are honest.**
   - Case 1 returned without ever exceeding 90% MV.
   - Case 2 returned a week before the staff recommendation.
   - Sprint volume was under-dosed at 40% of game value.
   - A low high-speed-running threshold (17 km/h) twice inflated the totals by accident.

   Real practice looks like this, and it shows where the framework bends.

What is weak:

1. **It is Matt Taberner's control-chaos continuum with a velocity layer added.** Harries credits Taberner himself. You already hold five Taberner papers (see `RTP_Constraints_Course/RESOURCES.md`). The course adds nothing new to the theory; its new value is the worked numbers.
2. **The complexity axis rests on older motor-learning theory, not ecological dynamics.** This matters most for Joe's course.
   - Blocked → serial → random practice is contextual interference, from the Schmidt information-processing tradition.
   - His "closed reactivity" example is a coach throwing a hand signal. That is a generic stimulus, not the information a player actually uses in a game, such as a defender's hips.
   - He mentions "constraints-based learning design" once, in Part 2, in one sentence, and never puts it into practice.
   - In this model, complexity is something added once intensity is safe. In an ecological model, the right information has to be present from the start and scaled, not switched on at Level 4.
3. **The progression criteria are almost all physical.** Healing time, pain, force benchmarks and % MV are all measured. The one behavioural criterion ("if they hesitate… they are not ready") is stated in Part 2 and never measured. That hesitation is exactly the subjective judgement Joe says he cannot defend to objective people.
4. **AFL is not American football.** AFL is continuous: about 13 km a game and about 200 m of very-high-speed running. Football is intermittent, position-specific and built around collision. The % MV logic transfers; the thresholds do not.
   - The 17/23/27 km/h bands and "% of game value" have to be re-derived for each position from Baylor GPS.
   - Many linemen may rarely or never reach a 27 km/h sprint threshold in a game. Check that in our data before assuming it either way.
5. **Contact is missing as a pillar.** Tackling appears once, as a word. For football, collision and contact (block, shed, tackle, hand-fight, stance start) is a fourth pillar. It is also where Joe's "I am not the right constraint" case sits: the lineman who needed real bodies.
6. **Evidence quality.** The benchmarks (80–85% Nordic, 1.8× body weight calf isometric, two exposures above 90%) are expert opinion and common practice, not results from trials. He says so himself ("varied opinions in the field"). Label them that way whenever they are used.
7. **He deliberately de-emphasised GPS** so the framework would work without it. Your job is GPS, so for you that is the part to reverse, not copy.

## 3. How it helps you understand the concepts

| Concept in the course | What you already have | The gap it fills for you |
|---|---|---|
| % MV bands per level | Each player's MV and speed zones in the Catapult pipeline | An agreed, measurable language with Athletic Medicine: "Level 3 means 75–85% of *his* MV" |
| 75–85% gate | Force plate and Nordic data (ForceDecks, NordBord) | A **decision gate** you can compute. This is Old Bull Lab 2D in practice, and it separates monitoring (a GPS trend) from testing (a gate check), which is Lab 2C |
| Linear → undulating | You already undulate load across the team week | The same logic applied to one returning player, anchored to the team's Tue/Wed high, Thu low pattern. Joe asked for this in his tool spec |
| High-speed / very-high-speed / sprint volume as % of game value | Game demands by position | A running "% of game" line per player that Joe can see, for example 40% (under-dosed) vs 70–80% (on track) |
| Eight intensity levers | Nothing formal | A shared checklist for why a drill is harder, and the input schema for Joe's drill-design tool |
| Control → chaos | Joe's course (Taberner, Gray, Myszka) | A clear view of where Harries stops and ecological dynamics begins (section 2, weakness 2) |

4. What would "% of game value" mean for a centre compared with a boundary corner?

- **Who uses it.** Joe. Jacob and Tim are the gatekeepers, so show it to them before it goes into use.
- **Why first.** It turns Harries' method into Baylor numbers without changing anyone's workflow. It needs no clinical sign-off because it is a calculator, not a clearance tool. Joe asked for exactly these numbers in his tool spec ("return-to-run and high-speed running for hamstrings").
- **Size.** One script against data you already have, rendered as a one-page PDF.
- **Target.** After the three items already queued, or swapped in if it is a better ship than one of them. That is your call.

1. **A football version of the intensity-lever table.** Keep Harries' eight dials. 14	# In Return to Run, Watch Them Run
15	
16	**What it is** — Moyer's complaint from years in an orthopaedic practice: rehab clinics treat a running injury (patellar pain, a hamstring strain) with generic exercises — TKEs, knee extensions, Nordics, bridges, isometrics, then a short-to-long running programme — **without ever watching the athlete run**. The pain goes, the athlete "goes back to running like crap", and the injury returns. His process instead: (1) gather **injury history, training background and current goals**; (2) know the **sport's demands**; (3) **watch and film them run** before choosing interventions; (4) **re-film after** the rehab block to see whether mechanics or left-right differences actually changed. He states that "gym strength is less important than how they apply force to the ground during running", so a running-specific test is essential for judging progress.
17	
18	**Why it works** — Clinical tests and gym strength measure capacities; sprinting is the task that injures. If the running pattern that loaded the tissue is unchanged, capacity gains may not protect it. Filming before and after gives a direct check that the task has changed, not just the tests. The logic is sound; his framing that "research indicates biomechanical analysis can predict injuries" overstates the evidence, which is mostly associations.
19	
20	**When to apply** — Every lower-limb soft-tissue RTP at Baylor: film the athlete's running at each progression stage (tempo, 75%, 90%, max), side and front, and compare with pre-injury film when it exists. Pair film with GPS max velocity and force-plate or NordBord asymmetry so the decision has both a task view and a capacity view. Moyer quotes that about a third of hamstring injuries recur, with the highest risk in the first two weeks back — the window where running film is most useful.
21	
22	**When NOT to apply** — Film shows *how* they run, not tissue readiness; it does not replace strength, range, imaging or clinical criteria, and "runs well" is not a clearance test. Changing mechanics during late rehab also adds a new stressor at a vulnerable time — record mechanics, but be careful about making big technique changes in the final days before clearance. His injury statistics (25–35% of team-sport injuries are hamstrings, "some show 50%") were quoted loosely.
23	
24	**Example** — A cornerback cleared on NordBord symmetry and pain-free isometrics is filmed at 90%. Side view shows his injured leg still swinging a long lever and landing further ahead than the other. Staff hold the progression one stage and add swing-leg work before max-velocity exposure.
25	
26	**Related** — [[claim--rtp-should-examine-the-movement-pattern-at-injury]] — the causal version of this (untested); this entry is the practice. [[claim--long-swing-lever-and-heel-strike-hamstring-hypothesis]]; [[principle--action-capacity-is-not-skill]] — agreement: capacity scores do not show how the task is performed.
27

3	Source: `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\09_PRO_DEV\SS_Course_OnFieldRTP\Video Transcripts\Part 1 - What every field sport rehab has in common.mp4`. Course lesson: https://www.sportsmith.co/course/fundamentals-of-on-field-rehabilitation/lessons/what-every-field-sport-rehab-has-in-common/. Duration: 00:08:49. Transcribed locally with faster-whisper small.en, CPU int8. Automated draft; names and technical terms may be misrecognized. Timestamps refer to the downloaded media.
4	
5	**00:00:00–00:00:10** Welcome to rehab running for field-based team sport. This course is about all things rehab
6	
7	**00:00:10–00:00:15** running and the on-field rehab processes I believe you should consider when returning
8	
9	**00:00:15–00:00:21** an athlete back from injury. In addition to fully rehabilitating the injured area, the
10	
11	**00:00:21–00:00:27** aim of rehab running or on-field rehab is to prepare the athlete to be capable of performing
12	
13	**00:00:27–00:00:32** the technical, the tactical and physical requirements of the sport. On-field rehab occurs during
14	
15	**00:00:32–00:00:38** the mid to late stages of rehab and it's a crucial period that connects to gym-based rehab
16	
17	**00:00:38–00:00:44** and the return to sport participation. It starts with an initial return to running and then
18	
19	**00:00:44–00:00:49** a gradual progression of an athlete's ability to perform all the locomotor actions required
20	
21	**00:00:49–00:00:53** of their sport. And we need to do this in a way that minimises the chance or the risk
22	
23	**00:00:53–00:00:59** of a negative reloading response such as an increase in symptoms or at worse a recurrence
24	
25	**00:00:59–00:01:06** and also in a way that considers the specificity of what we are preparing athletes for. Therefore
26	
27	**00:01:06–00:01:12** there are two major focus areas of any sound on-field rehab process that you should have
28	
29	**00:01:12–00:01:18** clarity on. You should know the specific physical and locomotor activities required of
30	
31	**00:01:18–00:01:23** the athlete in their sport and you should know how to progress the athlete's ability
32	
33	**00:01:23–00:01:31** to perform those physical and locomotor activities under the specific demands of that sport.
34	
35	**00:01:31–00:01:38** To make sure you have this clarity, in subsequent modules we will consider the universal locomotor
36	
37	**00:01:38–00:01:44** activities across all invasion-based team sports. We're going to consider where rehab
38	
39	**00:01:44–00:01:48** running fits in the return to play process. We're going to look at the different stages
40	
41	**00:01:48–00:01:54** of levels of on-field rehab and we're going to look at the major pillars of on-field rehab
42	
43	**00:01:54–00:01:59** including sub-maximal and maximal velocity running, multi-directional speed and agility
44	
45	**00:01:59–00:02:04** and sport specific skills. And we're going to look at how to progress the intensity and
46	
47	**00:02:04–00:02:10** complexity of those activities throughout the on-field rehab stages and lastly how to
48	
49	**00:02:10–00:02:15** apply this knowledge into our programming and session design. So to help bring some of this
50	
51	**00:02:15–00:02:20** information to life, we're going to use a case study example throughout the course. That
52	
53	**00:02:20–00:02:25** case is going to be a low-grade hamstring strain in a professional AFL player and he's
54	
55	**00:02:25–00:02:33** a defensive back. His max velocity is 34.2 kilometres per hour and on average, you can
56	
57	**00:02:33–00:02:37** see the information in the slide here, but he will cover around about 13 kilometres per
58	
59	**00:02:37–00:02:43** game, around about 1000 metres of the high-speed running per game and approximately 200 metres
60	
61	**00:02:43–00:02:49** of very high-speed running and in the vicinity of 40 to 50 accelerations or decelerations
62	
63	**00:02:49–00:02:55** per game. So please keep in mind this is just one example and of course with different injuries
64	
65	**00:02:55–00:03:00** of different severities and in different environments when those injuries will occur, we may do
66	
67	**00:03:00–00:03:04** things very differently but we're using this case study to bring some of this information
68	
69	**00:03:04–00:03:11** I suppose into a real world applied setting. Before you can put a framework together, you
70	
71	**00:03:11–00:03:17** need to have a systematic process to identify the specific requirements and demands of the
72	
73	**00:03:17–00:03:23** sport. And you need to be clear on what performance in that sport looks like. I find a useful
74	
75	**00:03:23–00:03:27** starting point in this process is to look at the technical, the tactical and the physical
76	
77	**00:03:27–00:03:33** domain requirements. Okay, so let's look at a really simple diagram outlining the technical,
78	
79	**00:03:33–00:03:37** the tactical and the physical domains of a sport. We're going to talk about football
80	
81	**00:03:37–00:03:43** for now. So the first thing we can see is there's a massive overlap across those domains.
82	
83	**00:03:43–00:03:47** We intuitively know this. We know that there's nothing done from a physical perspective like
84	
85	**00:03:47–00:03:54** a physical action that doesn't have a dual purpose for either a technical or tactical
86	
87	**00:03:54–00:03:59** purpose in the game. So that's really important for us to know. We could then go about listing
88	
89	**00:03:59–00:04:05** out all the actions in each of these domains to list things that the player would do.
90	
91	**00:04:05–00:04:09** Is that pressing up and down the field? Is that dribbling the ball? Is that passing the
92	
93	**00:04:09–00:04:15** ball to a teammate? Etc, etc. That would give us a really broad overview of the requirements
94	
95	**00:04:15–00:04:20** for performance in that particular sport, as I said, football. And then we can work backwards
96	
97	**00:04:20–00:04:25** from that and start to map out our on-field rehab process and our frameworks that will
98	
99	**00:04:25–00:04:29** help support us through the on-field rehab process. However, it is very easy to be
100	
101	**00:04:29–00:04:34** overwhelmed by the vast number of activities that contribute to performance in team-based
102	
103	**00:04:34–00:04:40** sports. You can further simplify this process by looking at the commonalities all of these
104	
105	**00:04:40–00:04:46** types of sports share. An invasion-based sport is a type of sport where two teams compete
106	
107	**00:04:46–00:04:51** to invade the opponent's territory, the objective scoring points typically getting
108	
109	**00:04:51–00:04:57** a ball into a goal area. Unsurprisingly, there are two primary tactical patterns involved
110	
111	**00:04:57–00:05:02** in all of these sports. Offense, where one team is trying to invade the other team's
112	
113	**00:05:02–00:05:09** space to score. And defence, where one team is trying to prevent the other team from invading
114	
115	**00:05:09–00:05:15** their space. When looking at locomotor tasks in these sports, there are many similarities
116	
117	**00:05:15–00:05:22** across the offence and defensive elements. And underpinning physical elements that facilitate
118	
119	**00:05:22–00:05:28** the successful execution of those offensive and defensive strategies. So let's look at
120	
121	**00:05:28–00:05:32** performance in an invasion-based sport. And we're going to broadly break this up into
122	
123	**00:05:32–00:05:36** offensive and defensive strategies. All right, so as you can see on the slide, let's start
124	
125	**00:05:36–00:05:43** with the offensive. And an offensive strategy or attacking phases of play, they can be broken
126	
127	**00:05:43–00:05:47** down into the tactical actions that might be performed, but also the technical. So those
128	
129	**00:05:47–00:05:53** tactical actions might be pressing up the field and might be running into space and might
130	
131	**00:05:53–00:05:57** be trying to get an overlapping situation there. Whereas the technical actions would
132	
133	**00:05:57–00:06:01** be, you know, running with the ball or moving with the ball, for example, whether that's
134	
135	**00:06:01–00:06:06** dribbling or carrying the ball, it's moving the ball by passing it to a teammate, throwing
136	
137	**00:06:06–00:06:13** it to a teammate, for example. And it's also catching or receiving the ball. So they're
138	
139	**00:06:13–00:06:17** really common technical and tactical actions across all invasion sports. And if we now
140	
141	**00:06:17–00:06:22** look at defensive actions or defensive tactical strategies and technical actions, we can
142	
143	**00:06:22–00:06:29** again see a lot of commonalities or similarities. So in tactical perspectives, we see covering,
144	
145	**00:06:29–00:06:34** we see closing space, we see retreating down the field. And technical actions we
146	
147	**00:06:34–00:06:39** see tackling of various kinds, and we see intercepting or contesting the possession
148	
149	**00:06:39–00:06:46** of the ball. Now, underpinning both those attacking and defensive strategies is a range
150	
151	**00:06:46–00:06:52** of common physical parameters or physical loadings. So we have our overall physical load,
152	
153	**00:06:52–00:06:57** and that might be, for example, the total distance we cover in a particular sport. It might be
154	
155	**00:06:57–00:07:02** the high speed running distance, the sprint distance, for example, the number of accelerations
156	
157	**00:07:02–00:07:06** or decelerations that would be covered in the game. So across the physical actions
158	
159	**00:07:06–00:07:11** that is common amongst these invasion based sports, we can see sprinting, we can see
160	
161	**00:07:11–00:07:15** changing direction, we can see accelerating, we can see decelerating. And we just see
162	
163	**00:07:15–00:07:19** that time and time again in these types of sports. Now, of course, there's going to be
164	
165	**00:07:19–00:07:25** really hyper specific movement patterns, and the exact total loading parameters will be
166	
167	**00:07:25–00:07:30** different across sports. However, these actual actions like the actual locomotive actions
168	
169	**00:07:30–00:07:35** don't change too much. There's a lot of similarities. So we can use them. And they
170	
171	**00:07:35–00:07:41** can be a great starting point for our on field rehab process. Therefore, you can consider
172	
173	**00:07:41–00:07:47** sprinting, accelerating, decelerating and change of direction to be primary locomotive
174	
175	**00:07:47–00:07:53** pillars of on field rehab, and use these categories of transferable locomotive
176	
177	**00:07:53–00:07:58** activities to any rehab running framework you create. You can also use your
178	
179	**00:07:58–00:08:03** understanding of common offensive and defensive actions to create progressively
180	
181	**00:08:03–00:08:08** contextual drills that require athletes to express locomotive activities for the
182	
183	**00:08:08–00:08:13** purpose of creating or closing space. With the commonalities in locomotive
184	
185	**00:08:13–00:08:17** actions across invasion based team sports, it is a little surprise that
186	
187	**00:08:17–00:08:22** numerous on field rehab frameworks have already been constructed around three
188	
189	**00:08:22–00:08:27** major themes submaximal and maximal velocity running multi directional speed
190	
191	**00:08:27–00:08:32** and agility and sport specific skills. In subsequent modules, we will take a look
192	
193	**00:08:32–00:08:37** at each of these pillars. But before we do that, let's turn our attention to
194	
195	**00:08:37–00:08:41** the process of moving from the gym based rehab to the on field rehab and
196	
197	**00:08:41–00:08:46** ultimately to transition into sport and why a framework can help you do this.
198

**00:02:10–00:02:15** apply this knowledge into our programming and session design. So to help bring some of this

**00:02:15–00:02:20** information to life, we're going to use a case study example throughout the course. That

**00:02:20–00:02:25** case is going to be a low-grade hamstring strain in a professional AFL player and he's

**00:02:25–00:02:33** a defensive back. His max velocity is 34.2 kilometres per hour and on average, you can

**00:02:33–00:02:37** see the information in the slide here, but he will cover around about 13 kilometres per

**00:02:37–00:02:43** game, around about 1000 metres of the high-speed running per game and approximately 200 metres

**00:02:43–00:02:49** of very high-speed running and in the vicinity of 40 to 50 accelerations or decelerations

**00:02:49–00:02:55** per game. So please keep in mind this is just one example and of course with different injuries

**00:02:55–00:03:00** of different severities and in different environments when those injuries will occur, we may do

**00:03:00–00:03:04** things very differently but we're using this case study to bring some of this information

**00:03:04–00:03:11** I suppose into a real world applied setting. Before you can put a framework together, you

**00:03:11–00:03:17** need to have a systematic process to identify the specific requirements and demands of the

**00:03:17–00:03:23** sport. And you need to be clear on what performance in that sport looks like. I find a useful

**00:03:23–00:03:27** starting point in this process is to look at the technical, the tactical and the physical

**00:03:27–00:03:33** domain requirements. Okay, so let's look at a really simple diagram outlining the technical,

**00:03:33–00:03:37** the tactical and the physical domains of a sport. We're going to talk about football

**00:03:37–00:03:43** for now. So the first thing we can see is there's a massive overlap across those domains.

**00:03:43–00:03:47** We intuitively know this. We know that there's nothing done from a physical perspective like

**00:03:47–00:03:54** a physical action that doesn't have a dual purpose for either a technical or tactical

**00:03:54–00:03:59** purpose in the game. So that's really important for us to know. We could then go about listing

**00:03:59–00:04:05** out all the actions in each of these domains to list things that the player would do.

**00:04:05–00:04:09** Is that pressing up and down the field? Is that dribbling the ball? Is that passing the

**00:04:09–00:04:15** ball to a teammate? Etc, etc. That would give us a really broad overview of the requirements

**00:04:15–00:04:20** for performance in that particular sport, as I said, football. And then we can work backwards

**00:04:20–00:04:25** from that and start to map out our on-field rehab process and our frameworks that will

**00:04:25–00:04:29** help support us through the on-field rehab process. However, it is very easy to be

**00:04:29–00:04:34** overwhelmed by the vast number of activities that contribute to performance in team-based

**00:04:34–00:04:40** sports. You can further simplify this process by looking at the commonalities all of these

**00:04:40–00:04:46** types of sports share. An invasion-based sport is a type of sport where two teams compete

**00:04:46–00:04:51** to invade the opponent's territory, the objective scoring points typically getting

**00:04:51–00:04:57** a ball into a goal area. Unsurprisingly, there are two primary tactical patterns involved

**00:04:57–00:05:02** in all of these sports. Offense, where one team is trying to invade the other team's

**00:05:02–00:05:09** space to score. And defence, where one team is trying to prevent the other team from invading

**00:05:09–00:05:15** their space. When looking at locomotor tasks in these sports, there are many similarities

**00:05:15–00:05:22** across the offence and defensive elements. And underpinning physical elements that facilitate

**00:05:22–00:05:28** the successful execution of those offensive and defensive strategies. So let's look at

**00:05:28–00:05:32** performance in an invasion-based sport. And we're going to broadly break this up into

**00:05:32–00:05:36** offensive and defensive strategies. All right, so as you can see on the slide, let's start

**00:05:36–00:05:43** with the offensive. And an offensive strategy or attacking phases of play, they can be broken

**00:05:43–00:05:47** down into the tactical actions that might be performed, but also the technical. So those

**00:05:47–00:05:53** tactical actions might be pressing up the field and might be running into space and might

**00:05:53–00:05:57** be trying to get an overlapping situation there. Whereas the technical actions would

**00:05:57–00:06:01** be, you know, running with the ball or moving with the ball, for example, whether that's

**00:06:01–00:06:06** dribbling or carrying the ball, it's moving the ball by passing it to a teammate, throwing

**00:06:06–00:06:13** it to a teammate, for example. And it's also catching or receiving the ball. So they're

**00:06:13–00:06:17** really common technical and tactical actions across all invasion sports. And if we now

**00:06:17–00:06:22** look at defensive actions or defensive tactical strategies and technical actions, we can

**00:06:22–00:06:29** again see a lot of commonalities or similarities. So in tactical perspectives, we see covering,

**00:06:29–00:06:34** we see closing space, we see retreating down the field. And technical actions we

**00:06:34–00:06:39** see tackling of various kinds, and we see intercepting or contesting the possession

**00:06:39–00:06:46** of the ball. Now, underpinning both those attacking and defensive strategies is a range

**00:06:46–00:06:52** of common physical parameters or physical loadings. So we have our overall physical load,

**00:06:52–00:06:57** and that might be, for example, the total distance we cover in a particular sport. It might be

**00:06:57–00:07:02** the high speed running distance, the sprint distance, for example, the number of accelerations

**00:07:02–00:07:06** or decelerations that would be covered in the game. So across the physical actions

**00:07:06–00:07:11** that is common amongst these invasion based sports, we can see sprinting, we can see

**00:07:11–00:07:15** changing direction, we can see accelerating, we can see decelerating. And we just see

**00:07:15–00:07:19** that time and time again in these types of sports. Now, of course, there's going to be

**00:07:19–00:07:25** really hyper specific movement patterns, and the exact total loading parameters will be

**00:07:25–00:07:30** different across sports. However, these actual actions like the actual locomotive actions

**00:07:30–00:07:35** don't change too much. There's a lot of similarities. So we can use them. And they

**00:07:35–00:07:41** can be a great starting point for our on field rehab process. Therefore, you can consider

**00:07:41–00:07:47** sprinting, accelerating, decelerating and change of direction to be primary locomotive

**00:07:47–00:07:53** pillars of on field rehab, and use these categories of transferable locomotive

**00:07:53–00:07:58** activities to any rehab running framework you create. You can also use your

**00:07:58–00:08:03** understanding of common offensive and defensive actions to create progressively

**00:08:03–00:08:08** contextual drills that require athletes to express locomotive activities for the

**00:08:08–00:08:13** purpose of creating or closing space. With the commonalities in locomotive

**00:08:13–00:08:17** actions across invasion based team sports, it is a little surprise that

**00:08:17–00:08:22** numerous on field rehab frameworks have already been constructed around three

**00:08:22–00:08:27** major themes submaximal and maximal velocity running multi directional speed

**00:08:27–00:08:32** and agility and sport specific skills. In subsequent modules, we will take a look

**00:08:32–00:08:37** at each of these pillars. But before we do that, let's turn our attention to

**00:08:37–00:08:41** the process of moving from the gym based rehab to the on field rehab and

**00:08:41–00:08:46** ultimately to transition into sport and why a framework can help you do this.
