# Part 1: What Every Field Sport Rehab Has in Common — Summary

**Source:** Downloaded Vimeo lesson, transcribed locally with faster-whisper small.en. The transcript is an automated draft and has not been checked word-for-word against the audio. Timestamps below refer to the video.

## Main point

On-field rehabilitation bridges gym-based rehabilitation and return to sport, preparing an athlete to handle the technical, tactical, and physical demands of their sport. The process should progress relevant movement demands while monitoring for adverse symptom responses or recurrence. The speaker says staff need clarity on two things: what physical and locomotor activities the sport requires, and how to progress an athlete's ability to perform those activities under sport-specific demands. (00:00–01:31)

## How the speaker builds the framework

- **Start with the sport’s demands.** The technical, tactical, and physical domains overlap. The speaker recommends mapping what athletes actually do, then working backward to build the rehabilitation process. (03:11–04:29)
- **Use common patterns in invasion sports.** Attacking examples include pressing upfield, running into space, carrying or passing the ball, and receiving it. Defending examples include covering, closing space, retreating, tackling, and intercepting. These are presented as recurring patterns across invasion-based team sports. (04:40–06:46)
- **Build around transferable locomotor actions.** Sprinting, accelerating, decelerating, and changing direction are identified as core movement demands. The speaker groups on-field work into submaximal and maximal velocity running, multidirectional speed and agility, and sport-specific skills. (06:46–08:32)
- **Contextualize drills.** Use the common attacking and defensive actions to build progressive drills in which athletes move to create or close space. (07:58–08:17)

## Case example and caveat

The course uses a professional AFL defensive back returning from a low-grade hamstring strain as a running example. The speaker cites match demands of about 13 km total distance, 1,000 m high-speed running, 200 m very-high-speed running, 40–50 accelerations/decelerations, and a 34.2 km/h maximum velocity. He explicitly describes it as one example; those values are not universal targets or a return-to-play standard. (02:15–03:11)

**Practical takeaway:** Start with the athlete’s sport-specific movement and skill demands, then build a staged progression from gym rehabilitation through on-field work toward sport participation. The video presents a framework, not an individualized clinical clearance protocol.

# Part 2 - On-field rehab frameworks: transcript

Source: `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\09_PRO_DEV\SS_Course_OnFieldRTP\Video Transcripts\Part 2 - On-field rehab frameworks.mp4`. Course lesson: https://www.sportsmith.co/course/fundamentals-of-on-field-rehabilitation/lessons/on-field-rehab-frameworks/. Duration: 00:10:54. Transcribed locally with faster-whisper small.en, CPU int8. Automated draft cross-checked against Vimeo captions on 2026-09-24. Platform captions and local speech recognition can both contain errors. Clear recognition errors were corrected and technical terms normalized; no independent human audio-listening pass was completed. Timestamps refer to the downloaded media.

**00:00:00–00:00:14** A framework is a structured system or a model that we can use to map out principles and methods

**00:00:14–00:00:20** for improving any aspect of training or rehab. They help standardise your practices by incorporating

**00:00:20–00:00:26** the evidence base and your personal experiences to guide or scaffold your decision making.

**00:00:26–00:00:32** They not only allow for consistency and quality assurance, but flexibility to adapt to the athlete

**00:00:32–00:00:39** in the injury context. So now let's look at some of the key benefits of having a framework and what

**00:00:39–00:00:45** the purpose of a framework is. So there are four in my mind. The first one is the fact that

**00:00:45–00:00:51** it allows us to take calculated risks. That is it probably acts as a bit of a guardrail or a guide

**00:00:51–00:00:57** so we don't fall into the trap of perhaps pushing an athlete too quickly and end up with a negative

**00:00:57–00:01:05** reloading response or worst case recurrence. The other main purpose of a framework is that if we

**00:01:05–00:01:11** align it closely to what the actual performance requirements of a sport are, it can help the

**00:01:11–00:01:18** preparedness of an athlete when they subsequently return to sport. The third one that's really

**00:01:18–00:01:23** important is it provides a lot of flexibility for us to individualise the rehab process.

**00:01:23–00:01:29** So it can't be too rigid, so it's not a protocol. Again, a framework for me would be a guide,

**00:01:30–00:01:35** not a step-by-step process. And the last one which is really important is that it creates

**00:01:35–00:01:40** a lot of efficiencies and consistencies in how we put our programs together, how we prescribe

**00:01:40–00:01:45** certain things throughout the on-field rehab process and also really importantly our decision

**00:01:45–00:01:49** making process. I think for me this has been one of the main benefits of having a range of

**00:01:49–00:01:56** frameworks for on-field rehab is that I can quickly make decisions on the fly as things happen

**00:01:56–00:02:01** and as a result I can tell that there's a higher level of trust between myself and the athlete.

**00:02:01–00:02:07** Ultimately, regardless of the exact specifics of whichever on-field rehab framework you deem

**00:02:07–00:02:14** suitable, they are all built upon the basis of systematic progression of volume, intensity

**00:02:14–00:02:20** and complexity of locomotor actions that are relevant to the sport. A number of frameworks

**00:02:20–00:02:26** to guide this already exist and outline stages or levels that generally move from the gym,

**00:02:27–00:02:32** base rehab to the on-field rehab and then a series of transitional levels back to sport

**00:02:32–00:02:37** participation. Splitting the on-field rehab process into a number of levels an athlete

**00:02:37–00:02:42** moves through, it's really useful as a way to organise and provide structure to the return

**00:02:42–00:02:48** to running process. These on-field rehab levels scaffold the gradual stressing of an athlete's

**00:02:48–00:02:54** ability to perform the specific locomotor actions required of their sport. So now let's look at

**00:02:54–00:03:00** splitting the on-field rehab process into a number of sub-stages or levels. We can think about these

**00:03:00–00:03:06** as aligning to either the early, the mid or the later parts of the rehab process. So the early

**00:03:06–00:03:11** stage, that's when we're still in the gym, you know we haven't yet progressed onto the field

**00:03:11–00:03:18** mid-stage though, we now might want to chunk that into three levels of on-field rehab levels one,

**00:03:18–00:03:24** two and three and then finally in the late stage of rehab we might start to look at

**00:03:24–00:03:30** on-field rehab levels four and five. So now let's look at our hamstring case study, so that low

**00:03:30–00:03:34** grade hamstring and when would they do their sessions. So with this one because it's quite

**00:03:34–00:03:39** a minor injury they're only going to do a single session in each of the on-field rehab

**00:03:39–00:03:43** levels. Now of course with a more severe injury or different type of injury or a different

**00:03:43–00:03:49** context you know you may do a number of sessions in each level before moving on but this particular

**00:03:49–00:03:54** example they're going to do sessions one, two and three in on-field rehab one, two and three

**00:03:54–00:03:59** and they're going to do session four and five in on-field rehab four and five and then they'll

**00:03:59–00:04:05** actually then have as part of their return to training transition they would do session six

**00:04:05–00:04:10** and session seven in training with the team or the squad and then finally session eight would

**00:04:10–00:04:16** actually be their return to play. To systematically progress intensity and complexity of locomotor

**00:04:16–00:04:22** actions you need to be clear on what the specific things are that need to be progressed.

**00:04:23–00:04:28** As mentioned in the previous module the key locomotor actions we need to restore

**00:04:28–00:04:35** ability to perform are sprinting, accelerating, decelerating, changing direction and also running

**00:04:35–00:04:40** at sub-maximal speeds. Then you need to have an understanding of how intensity and complexity can

**00:04:40–00:04:48** be generally increased. So if we think about how we can grade up the intensity and the complexity

**00:04:48–00:04:55** of the on-field rehab process which are our two primary objectives. So we need to split out

**00:04:55–00:05:01** initially thinking about intensity into two areas. So I think we should be thinking about

**00:05:01–00:05:07** the earlier parts of our on-field rehab process as a competency focus.

**00:05:10–00:05:15** So we're introducing movements, we're reintroducing the athlete to different locomotor

**00:05:15–00:05:20** actions that they would need to do, we're progressing them up to a sub-maximal level

**00:05:20–00:05:26** and as of course it is a transition, you know it's not a straight you know stop and go,

**00:05:26–00:05:31** it's a continuum here. We're going to move across towards a bit more of a capacity focus.

**00:05:34–00:05:39** Now we're still going to be of course going from sub-maximal intensities all the way up

**00:05:39–00:05:45** to maximal intensities but we can start to shift our emphasis towards building capacity

**00:05:45–00:05:51** to do those locomotor actions under some additional loading and metabolic and mechanical demands.

**00:05:53–00:06:00** In regards to complexity we can think about that as a you know a controller chaos type continuum

**00:06:00–00:06:07** as Matt Taberner's work is you know so eloquently put together and at the start we want high control.

**00:06:07–00:06:18** Another way to think about this is risk. So we want in this period of time in on-field rehab

**00:06:18–00:06:22** we want quite a low risk situation. So we're going to control a lot of things, we're going

**00:06:22–00:06:26** to make sure we don't expose the player to something that they're not yet ready for

**00:06:26–00:06:29** and that we haven't I suppose accounted for in our programming design

**00:06:30–00:06:35** and as a continuum again we're going to move across towards high chaos.

**00:06:37–00:06:47** Well excuse the spelling there it made a little mistake but what we're looking for this high

**00:06:47–00:06:54** chaos instead of low risk we want high risk situations and essentially that's what we're

**00:06:54–00:06:59** trying to do throughout the on-field rehab process. We're trying to get to a point of having

**00:07:00–00:07:07** over on the right hand side high intensity but also high complexity of training and

**00:07:07–00:07:11** we can't do that without taking risk we just need to figure out how we're going to get them

**00:07:11–00:07:17** from those low risk settings through to high risk settings. Many will be familiar with the work of

**00:07:17–00:07:22** Matt Taberner and his on-field rehab framework which he describes as several stages along a

**00:07:22–00:07:27** controlled chaos continuum. His framework has five stages of progression from high control

**00:07:27–00:07:33** or low intensity towards high chaos being high intensity. Control that's a high level

**00:07:33–00:07:39** structure on the behavior the actions in the movement i.e. a controlled situation whereas chaos

**00:07:39–00:07:45** it's unpredictable it's unpredictable behavior actions movement it appears as random or reactive

**00:07:45–00:07:51** i.e. chaos. During the early on-field rehab levels the complexity of the environment will

**00:07:51–00:07:56** be low and highly controlled whereas through the later levels you'll be looking to structure

**00:07:56–00:08:00** situations that increase the unpredictability or chaotic nature of the environment.

**00:08:01–00:08:06** When you think about increasing the complexity of an environment you'll essentially need to be

**00:08:06–00:08:10** applying a constraints-based learning design to your on-field rehab activities.

**00:08:11–00:08:18** In simple terms this concept merely describes a dynamic interaction between the individual the

**00:08:18–00:08:22** environment and the tasks they are doing at the time. So we can change the environmental

**00:08:22–00:08:28** relevancy of our drills by manipulating an innumerable number of variables and that's

**00:08:28–00:08:34** going to manipulate our drill whatever we decide that drill is down the control end of the chaos

**00:08:34–00:08:39** or control to chaos continuum or up to the far end and create high chaos really unpredictable

**00:08:39–00:08:44** environments for the athlete to perform under. One of the common misunderstandings i see with

**00:08:44–00:08:49** the control to chaos continuum is that people assume that as you move from one on-field

**00:08:49–00:08:55** rehab level to the next that automatically every activity in that next level is performed

**00:08:55–00:09:00** that increasingly chaotic environment but that's not true there's going to be certain things and

**00:09:00–00:09:06** certain locomotor actions that we are still progressing along an intensity continuum we're

**00:09:06–00:09:11** moving from sub-maximal to maximal intensities and we're going to want to do those things

**00:09:11–00:09:15** in a much more controlled environment but there'll be other actions and other things we'll have

**00:09:15–00:09:19** already developed where we may be much more comfortable with increasing the environmental

**00:09:19–00:09:25** complexity in which they're performed right so what actually happens is over time there's a

**00:09:25–00:09:32** gradual progression towards more chaotic environments of course as our amount of work

**00:09:32–00:09:36** is done in a more controlled environment will decrease but i think it's important distinction

**00:09:36–00:09:40** to make that just because you are moving through the on-field rehab process doesn't mean

**00:09:40–00:09:47** everything must be done in a chaotic environment. It is for this reason you need to think of

**00:09:47–00:09:53** intensity and complexity as two equally important objectives of the on-field rehab process with

**00:09:53–00:09:59** the very end stage of on-field rehab and the initial return to training achieving both high

**00:09:59–00:10:04** intensity and high complexity exposing the athletes to those high intensity and complexity

**00:10:04–00:10:10** environments is an absolute must they need to show us they have restored the ability the

**00:10:10–00:10:15** confidence and the willingness to choose the right actions in the right environment in a

**00:10:15–00:10:20** competitive situation such as not hesitating to accelerate through a gap in the defence

**00:10:20–00:10:25** or performing a high intensity acceleration to chase another athlete in a small-sided game

**00:10:26–00:10:31** while sometimes this is overlooked my personal belief is this competitive element during the

**00:10:31–00:10:37** late or end stage rehab is critical to successful return to play outcomes it's hard for me to think

**00:10:37–00:10:43** of a situation where i would not want an athlete to confidently perform all those high intensity

**00:10:43–00:10:49** locomotor actions in highly competitive training situations before they return to play

# Part 2 - On-field rehab frameworks: summary

**Lesson:** [On-field rehab frameworks](https://www.sportsmith.co/course/fundamentals-of-on-field-rehabilitation/lessons/on-field-rehab-frameworks/)  
**Video length:** 10:54  
**Source:** Locally generated transcript from the downloaded Vimeo video. The automated transcript was cross-checked against Vimeo captions and clear errors were corrected. A human audio-listening pass is still needed for word-for-word verification.

## Main idea

A rehabilitation framework is a flexible structure for applying evidence and practitioner experience to decisions. It gives the clinician a consistent way to progress an athlete while leaving room to adapt to injury severity, the athlete, and the sport context. It is a guide for decisions, not a fixed protocol.

## Why use a framework

- It provides guardrails for taking calculated risks and helps avoid progressing too quickly, which could produce a poor reloading response or recurrence (00:00:45–00:01:05).
- It can improve readiness for sport when its demands align with the sport’s actual performance requirements (00:01:05–00:01:18).
- It supports individualized rehabilitation rather than a rigid step-by-step prescription (00:01:18–00:01:35).
- It improves consistency and efficiency in programming and decision making; a shared structure can also build athlete trust (00:01:35–00:02:01).

## How progression is organized

Progress rehabilitation systematically by increasing the **volume, intensity, and complexity** of sport-relevant locomotor actions. The course describes a transition from gym-based rehabilitation, through on-field levels, into team training and return to play (00:02:01–00:02:54).

The example low-grade hamstring case progresses through on-field levels 1–5, then two team-training sessions, then return to play. The speaker notes that more severe or different injuries may require multiple sessions at a level; the example uses one session per level (00:03:24–00:04:16).

The actions to restore include submaximal running, sprinting, acceleration, deceleration, and change of direction (00:04:16–00:04:40). The clinician should separately consider two progression aims:

- **Intensity/capacity:** early work emphasizes competency and reintroducing actions, then shifts toward building capacity under greater metabolic and mechanical demands, progressing from submaximal toward maximal effort (00:04:40–00:05:51).
- **Complexity/environment:** progress along a controlled-to-chaotic continuum. Start with predictable, low-risk conditions; later introduce more unpredictable, reactive, sport-like situations (00:05:53–00:08:00).

The lesson connects environmental design to constraints-based learning: manipulate the interaction among athlete, task, and environment to make drills more or less predictable and sport-relevant (00:08:01–00:08:44).

## Practical caution and end-stage target

Intensity and environmental complexity are related but distinct. Advancing an athlete to a later level does **not** mean every action must immediately be performed in a chaotic setting. Newly progressed actions may still need a controlled environment while already-developed actions are challenged with more complexity (00:08:44–00:09:47).

By the end of on-field rehabilitation and in the first return-to-training exposures, the athlete should demonstrate both high intensity and high complexity. The speaker emphasizes confidence and willingness to select appropriate actions in competitive situations—for example, accelerating through a gap or chasing another player in a small-sided game—as important preparation for return to play (00:09:47–00:10:49).

## Takeaway

Use the framework to make progression and risk visible: rebuild the required actions, then layer intensity and environmental demands in a deliberate, individualized way. Before return to play, expose the athlete to demanding, competitive situations and confirm that they can perform the relevant actions confidently.

1	# Part 3 — Linear submaximal & maximal running progressions
2	
3	**Video ID:** 1106177506  
4	**Duration:** 25:49.8  
5	**Basis:** Corrected local ASR, checked against the player’s autogenerated transcript.  
6	**Scope:** The percentages and performance values below are the lecturer’s teaching examples, not universal clearance thresholds.
7	
8	## Main points
9	
10	- Progress running exposure deliberately from jogging to running, striding, and sprinting. Faster running raises vertical ground-reaction force, force application rate, muscle activity, and hip, knee, and ankle power demands.
11	- The lecturer describes speed increases at lower velocities as coming mainly from longer strides, with greater ankle contribution; near striding and sprinting, further speed gains rely more on stride frequency and hip contribution. This makes the injury area relevant when choosing and progressing drills.
12	- Dribble walks/runs, transitions, A-skips, low-intensity pogos, and scissor shuffles/bounds reintroduce upright running positions, coordination, stiffness, and repetitive contacts. They can remain in warm-ups as preparation through the rehab process.
13	
14	## Progression and readiness
15	
16	- The example on-field levels progress approximately from 50–70% of max velocity (Level 1), 70–75% (Level 2), 75–85% (Level 3), 85–95% (Level 4), and above 95% toward 100% (Level 5).
17	- Before beginning linear running, the lecturer expects suitable range of motion, minimal pain or swelling, adequate local endurance/general strength, and the ability to tolerate dynamic force production and repetitive impact through preparation drills.
18	- Before moving above roughly 75–85% max velocity, consider adequate time for healing, symptom response to prior running sessions, and injury-specific force capacity. Examples given are hamstring eccentric strength via Nordic testing and seated calf isometric strength for a calf injury. He suggests around 80–85% of pre-injury output or, for seated calf peak force, a benchmark around 1.7–1.8 times body weight. Hopping/reactive-strength work can inform the athlete’s ability to produce high force quickly.
19	
20	## Session design examples
21	
22	- At lower speeds, fixed-distance repeats with a target completion time give the athlete and coach a controllable average speed. A 60 m repeat in 12 seconds is about 18 km/h average; peak speed will be somewhat higher.
23	- The hamstring case study begins with steady 60 m running progressions. Session 1 uses four reps each at 13, 12, and 11 seconds (about 16.6, 18, and 19.5 km/h average). Session 2 uses two reps at each progressively faster time (12, 11, 10.5, 10, and 9.5 seconds), targeting about 66–69% max velocity for that athlete. These are illustrative prescriptions.
24	- The lecturer prefers moving beyond steady-state repeats after approximately 70–75%, using “broken strides” with acceleration, speed-maintenance, and deceleration phases. One 60 m example divides the distance into 20 m for each phase; phase lengths can change to adjust acceleration demand. Stopwatch timing provides immediate feedback, with GPS/video tools as supporting measures.
25	- He describes a mostly linear session-to-session increase through early rehab, then an undulating progression around 80–85% and above, depending on injury severity, time, and context. In the example, he wants at least one and probably two exposures above 90% max velocity before return to training/play, while explicitly saying the exact number depends on the athlete and setting.
26	- Later-stage prescriptions should allow a comfortable, confident speed within a planned bandwidth. Do not force speed increases or hold the athlete below an appropriate target without reason; discuss how the athlete felt and what the coach observed between reps.
27

# Part 3 — Linear submaximal & maximal running progressions

**Video ID:** 1106177506  
**Duration:** 25:49.8  
**Basis:** Corrected local ASR, checked against the player’s autogenerated transcript.  
**Scope:** The percentages and performance values below are the lecturer’s teaching examples, not universal clearance thresholds.

## Main points

- Progress running exposure deliberately from jogging to running, striding, and sprinting. Faster running raises vertical ground-reaction force, force application rate, muscle activity, and hip, knee, and ankle power demands.
- The lecturer describes speed increases at lower velocities as coming mainly from longer strides, with greater ankle contribution; near striding and sprinting, further speed gains rely more on stride frequency and hip contribution. This makes the injury area relevant when choosing and progressing drills.
- Dribble walks/runs, transitions, A-skips, low-intensity pogos, and scissor shuffles/bounds reintroduce upright running positions, coordination, stiffness, and repetitive contacts. They can remain in warm-ups as preparation through the rehab process.

## Progression and readiness

- The example on-field levels progress approximately from 50–70% of max velocity (Level 1), 70–75% (Level 2), 75–85% (Level 3), 85–95% (Level 4), and above 95% toward 100% (Level 5).
- Before beginning linear running, the lecturer expects suitable range of motion, minimal pain or swelling, adequate local endurance/general strength, and the ability to tolerate dynamic force production and repetitive impact through preparation drills.
- Before moving above roughly 75–85% max velocity, consider adequate time for healing, symptom response to prior running sessions, and injury-specific force capacity. Examples given are hamstring eccentric strength via Nordic testing and seated calf isometric strength for a calf injury. He suggests around 80–85% of pre-injury output or, for seated calf peak force, a benchmark around 1.7–1.8 times body weight. Hopping/reactive-strength work can inform the athlete’s ability to produce high force quickly.

## Session design examples

- At lower speeds, fixed-distance repeats with a target completion time give the athlete and coach a controllable average speed. A 60 m repeat in 12 seconds is about 18 km/h average; peak speed will be somewhat higher.
- The hamstring case study begins with steady 60 m running progressions. Session 1 uses four reps each at 13, 12, and 11 seconds (about 16.6, 18, and 19.5 km/h average). Session 2 uses two reps at each progressively faster time (12, 11, 10.5, 10, and 9.5 seconds), targeting about 66–69% max velocity for that athlete. These are illustrative prescriptions.
- The lecturer prefers moving beyond steady-state repeats after approximately 70–75%, using “broken strides” with acceleration, speed-maintenance, and deceleration phases. One 60 m example divides the distance into 20 m for each phase; phase lengths can change to adjust acceleration demand. Stopwatch timing provides immediate feedback, with GPS/video tools as supporting measures.
- He describes a mostly linear session-to-session increase through early rehab, then an undulating progression around 80–85% and above, depending on injury severity, time, and context. In the example, he wants at least one and probably two exposures above 90% max velocity before return to training/play, while explicitly saying the exact number depends on the athlete and setting.
- Later-stage prescriptions should allow a comfortable, confident speed within a planned bandwidth. Do not force speed increases or hold the athlete below an appropriate target without reason; discuss how the athlete felt and what the coach observed between reps.

## Accuracy notes

The local transcript and the player’s autogenerated VTT have 95.0% normalized word-sequence similarity (4,550 VTT words; 4,523 ASR words). The local transcript clarified several garbled caption/ASR terms, including running gait, eccentric strength, seated calf isometric, and km/h units. 1	# Part 6 — Case studies
2	
3	**Video ID:** 1106275831  
4	**Duration:** 46:29  
5	**Basis:** Independent ASR checked against the player’s autogenerated captions.  
6	**Scope:** Four AFL rehabilitation cases illustrate application of the course framework. Their timelines, exposures, and outcomes are descriptive examples, not validated return to play criteria.
7	
8	## Framework used in each case
9	
10	The lecturer reviews the timeline and loading pattern, maximum velocity progression, multidirectional speed and agility, and sport specific skill exposure. He emphasizes how **volume, intensity, complexity, and training integration** changed over time. He also points out departures from the intended plan and the role of injury history, medical judgment, schedule, and athlete response.
11	
12	## Four cases
13	
14	| Case | Reported return to play | Distinctive progression and constraint |
15	| --- | --- | --- |
16	| Proximal hamstring strain | Day 28 | Six rehab running sessions, then partial and full training. Running moved from timed repeats to strides and faster efforts. The athlete did not reach the desired exposure above 90% maximum velocity before play; the lecturer attributes this partly to timing pressure and says he would have preferred more sprint load. |
17	| Hamstring injury with adductor involvement | Day 30 | Running intensity rose across early sessions and later alternated moderate and high exposures. The athlete had two sessions above 90% maximum velocity. One high speed running session overshot its planned volume, while another high intensity exposure fell below the lecturer’s target. Return to play occurred one week earlier than the medical and performance team recommended. |
18	| Recurrent lateral soleus strain | Day 44 | The team delayed return by a week to add training exposure. Running resumed after a longer off legs period and then occurred about twice weekly, with extended recovery between sessions. Later sessions repeatedly exceeded 90% maximum velocity, while high speed running volume was held lower to leave room for multidirectional and sport skill work. |
19	| Grade 3 MCL sprain with meniscal involvement | Day 49 | Bracing and joint recovery delayed change of direction work. Straight line running advanced first; controlled cuts and braking followed, then reactive and competitive drills. The lecturer says a second exposure above 90% maximum velocity would have been preferable before play. |
20

# Part 6 — Case studies

**Video ID:** 1106275831  
**Duration:** 46:29  
**Basis:** Independent ASR checked against the player’s autogenerated captions.  
**Scope:** Four AFL rehabilitation cases illustrate application of the course framework. Their timelines, exposures, and outcomes are descriptive examples, not validated return to play criteria.

## Framework used in each case

The lecturer reviews the timeline and loading pattern, maximum velocity progression, multidirectional speed and agility, and sport specific skill exposure. He emphasizes how **volume, intensity, complexity, and training integration** changed over time. He also points out departures from the intended plan and the role of injury history, medical judgment, schedule, and athlete response.

## Four cases

| Case | Reported return to play | Distinctive progression and constraint |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Proximal hamstring strain | Day 28 | Six rehab running sessions, then partial and full training. Running moved from timed repeats to strides and faster efforts. The athlete did not reach the desired exposure above 90% maximum velocity before play; the lecturer attributes this partly to timing pressure and says he would have preferred more sprint load. |
| Hamstring injury with adductor involvement | Day 30 | Running intensity rose across early sessions and later alternated moderate and high exposures. The athlete had two sessions above 90% maximum velocity. One high speed running session overshot its planned volume, while another high intensity exposure fell below the lecturer’s target. Return to play occurred one week earlier than the medical and performance team recommended. |
| Recurrent lateral soleus strain | Day 44 | The team delayed return by a week to add training exposure. Running resumed after a longer off legs period and then occurred about twice weekly, with extended recovery between sessions. Later sessions repeatedly exceeded 90% maximum velocity, while high speed running volume was held lower to leave room for multidirectional and sport skill work. |
| Grade 3 MCL sprain with meniscal involvement | Day 49 | Bracing and joint recovery delayed change of direction work. Straight line running advanced first; controlled cuts and braking followed, then reactive and competitive drills. The lecturer says a second exposure above 90% maximum velocity would have been preferable before play. |

## Practical takeaways

- The cases use the same overall pillars, but the order and dose of running, cutting, and skills differ with tissue constraints and injury history.
- Running speed, high speed volume, cutting demand, and skill complexity do not all need to rise together. The examples deliberately shift emphasis between them across sessions.
- Planned and achieved exposures should be recorded separately. The lecturer calls out overshoots, missed sprint targets, and schedule driven compromises even when the athletes returned to play.

# Invasion-Sport Locomotor Pillars

**What it is** — Harries' starting point for building any on-field rehab process: map a sport's technical, tactical and physical domains, then simplify by using what invasion-based team sports (football, soccer, rugby, AFL) have in common. Every invasion sport reduces to two tactical patterns, offense (creating space: pressing forward, overlapping, running into space; technically: moving/passing/catching the ball) and defense (closing space: covering, retreating, closing down; technically: tackling, intercepting, contesting possession) (~03:33-06:46). Underneath both are the same physical actions: sprinting, accelerating, decelerating and changing direction. He names these four as the **primary locomotor pillars of on-field rehab**, usable as a starting template "to any rehab running framework you create" regardless of sport (~07:41-08:22).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: the exact loading numbers differ by sport, but the actual locomotor actions "don't change too much" across invasion sports, so building a rehab framework around them is a transferable shortcut instead of having to model every sport's full technical/tactical catalogue from scratch (~07:19-07:41).

**When to apply** — Use as the skeleton for any Baylor RTP conversation with Athletic Medicine: whatever the sport or position, the questions are the same four - can this athlete sprint, accelerate, decelerate and change direction at the required intensity, in an environment as complex as competition. It gives Applied Performance and Athletic Medicine a shared, sport-agnostic starting vocabulary before adding position-specific detail (GPS zones, skill demands).

**When NOT to apply** — Harries' own case-study sport is AFL, an unusually continuous, low-collision invasion game. Two gaps matter for Baylor football specifically: (1) **contact is missing as a pillar.** Tackling appears once, as a single word, never developed into its own progression. For football, collision and contact (block, shed, tackle, hand-fight, stance start) functions as a fourth pillar with its own dosage question, and this course gives it none. (2) The four pillars are a taxonomy of locomotor actions, not a testing or clearance protocol; they tell you what to progress, not how much force production or healing time is required before progressing it (see [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]] for that layer). Do not treat "the four pillars are covered" as equivalent to "the athlete is ready."

**Example** — A returning offensive lineman needs sprint/accel/decel/COD rebuilt like any other position, but the highest-risk gap in his return is a pillar this course never names: reintroducing collision tolerance. That has to be built separately, in coordination with position coaching, not inferred from his running progression.

**Related** — [[framework--on-field-rehab-levels-with-mv-bands]] (how the levels operationalize these pillars); Baylor's own documented gap that GPS/load thresholds are not yet sport- or position-specific (`method-baseline.md`, Load monitoring and GPS).

# A Framework Is a Guide, Not a Protocol

**What it is** — Harries lists four reasons to build an on-field rehab framework rather than freelance each case: (1) it acts as a guardrail against progressing an athlete too fast into a negative reloading response or recurrence; (2) aligning it to the sport's actual performance requirements improves an athlete's preparedness on return; (3) it stays flexible enough to individualize the rehab, because "it can't be too rigid... a framework for me would be a guide, not a step-by-step process"; (4) it creates efficiency and consistency in programming and in-the-moment decisions, which in his experience raises trust between practitioner and athlete (~00:39-02:01).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: a framework externalizes the decision logic (what to progress, in what order, under what conditions) so decisions under time pressure are faster and more defensible, without pretending every case fits the same fixed sequence.

**When to apply** — Use this as the pitch for why Applied Performance should hand Athletic Medicine a shared decision structure (levels, gates, exit criteria) rather than case-by-case verbal negotiation each time an athlete nears return. It is also the justification for building the framework at all, before any of the specific numbers below.

**When NOT to apply** — A framework that hardens into a fixed protocol defeats its own stated purpose. If Applied Performance builds phased levels and % MV gates for Baylor, they need to stay adjustable to injury severity, athlete history, season timing and organizational culture, per Harries' own repeated point in the exit-rule discussion (see [[heuristic--two-exposures-above-90-percent-mv-exit-rule]]) that he "can't tell you whether you need one, two, or seven" exposures - that answer is context-dependent, not fixed by the framework.

**Example** — Two hamstring cases in Part 6 used the same levels and pillars but different session frequencies, interval formats and undulation patterns because of different injury histories (see [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] vs [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]]); the framework held, the prescription did not.

**Related** — [[framework--intensity-complexity-two-independent-axes]]

# Intensity and Complexity as Two Independent Axes

**What it is** — Harries frames on-field rehab progression along two separate continuums that must both be advanced but do not have to move together. **Intensity** runs from a competency focus (reintroducing movements, building toward submaximal) to a capacity focus (submaximal through maximal, under added metabolic/mechanical demand). **Complexity** runs along what he explicitly credits as Matt Taberner's control-to-chaos continuum: control means high structure, predictable behavior/actions/movement (low risk); chaos means unpredictable, random or reactive behavior (high risk) (~04:48-08:00). Early on-field rehab levels are low-complexity and highly controlled; later levels deliberately build unpredictability. The **explicit misconception he corrects**: moving to a later on-field rehab level does not mean every drill in that level becomes more chaotic. Some locomotor actions are still climbing the intensity continuum (submaximal to maximal) and need a controlled environment even at a late stage, while other, already-developed actions can be pushed into more complex environments sooner (~08:44-09:47). By the end of on-field rehab, the target is both high intensity and high complexity simultaneously.

**Why it works** — Treating intensity and complexity as one variable causes two failure modes: pushing speed and unpredictability up together (risking a reload injury before the athlete can handle either alone), or holding both down together (leaving the athlete underprepared for the chaos of competition even though physically capable). Separating them lets a practitioner grade each independently and combine them deliberately only when both are ready.

**When to apply** — Use this distinction explicitly with Athletic Medicine and coaching staff: "he's ready for near-max speed but not yet ready for it in an unpredictable drill" is a defensible, gradeable statement under this framework, whereas "he's at level 4" alone is not. Baylor's own control-chaos foundation is Taberner's own published work already in the library (see Related) - Harries adds nothing new to the theory here; his contribution is packaging it with the specific %MV numbers (see [[framework--on-field-rehab-levels-with-mv-bands]]).

**When NOT to apply** — The complexity axis as Harries operationalizes it rests on an older, information-processing model of motor learning (blocked-to-serial-to-random practice, described in Part 5; see [[framework--practice-structure-block-serial-random-by-level]]), not on ecological dynamics/representative learning design. His example of "closed reactivity" is a coach throwing a hand signal - a generic, arbitrary stimulus, not the game-relevant information a player actually reads (a defender's hips, a gap opening). He names "constraints-based learning design" once, in this same module, and never operationalizes it. In this model, complexity is switched on once intensity is judged safe; in an ecological model, representative information should be present and scaled from the start, not withheld until Level 4. This is a genuine theoretical gap, flagged here as **contested** against the library's ecological-dynamics sources, not a reason to discard the intensity/complexity distinction itself, which still holds.

**Example** — A hamstring athlete at 82% max velocity with force benchmarks not yet cleared should still run in a controlled, closed environment even if his skill work has already moved to a positional, semi-random drill; conversely, an athlete cleared on force benchmarks but still hesitant in decision-making needs complexity pushed even at a plateaued running intensity.

**Related** — [[research-papers/taberner-2022-contextual-considerations-using-the-control-chaos-continuum-for-return-to-sport-in-elite-f]] (Taberner's own control-chaos continuum, the framework Harries is built on: suggested reciprocal link, "applied and re-dosed by a Sportsmith practitioner course, see on-field-rtp--harries"); [[research-papers/taberner-2019-physical-preparation-and-return-to-sport-of-the-football-player-with-a-tibia-fibula-fractu]]; [[skill-acquisition/enhancing-skill--myszka/framework--nonlinear-pedagogy-and-constraint-classes]] and [[skill-acquisition/enhancing-skill--myszka/principle--representative-design]] (the ecological-dynamics alternative to Harries' complexity operationalization); [[framework--practice-structure-block-serial-random-by-level]]

# Intensity and Complexity as Two Independent Axes

**What it is** — Harries frames on-field rehab progression along two separate continuums that must both be advanced but do not have to move together. **Intensity** runs from a competency focus (reintroducing movements, building toward submaximal) to a capacity focus (submaximal through maximal, under added metabolic/mechanical demand). **Complexity** runs along what he explicitly credits as Matt Taberner's control-to-chaos continuum: control means high structure, predictable behavior/actions/movement (low risk); chaos means unpredictable, random or reactive behavior (high risk) (~04:48-08:00). Early on-field rehab levels are low-complexity and highly controlled; later levels deliberately build unpredictability. The **explicit misconception he corrects**: moving to a later on-field rehab level does not mean every drill in that level becomes more chaotic. Some locomotor actions are still climbing the intensity continuum (submaximal to maximal) and need a controlled environment even at a late stage, while other, already-developed actions can be pushed into more complex environments sooner (~08:44-09:47). By the end of on-field rehab, the target is both high intensity and high complexity simultaneously.

**Why it works** — Treating intensity and complexity as one variable causes two failure modes: pushing speed and unpredictability up together (risking a reload injury before the athlete can handle either alone), or holding both down together (leaving the athlete underprepared for the chaos of competition even though physically capable). Separating them lets a practitioner grade each independently and combine them deliberately only when both are ready.

**When to apply** — Use this distinction explicitly with Athletic Medicine and coaching staff: "he's ready for near-max speed but not yet ready for it in an unpredictable drill" is a defensible, gradeable statement under this framework, whereas "he's at level 4" alone is not. Baylor's own control-chaos foundation is Taberner's own published work already in the library (see Related) - Harries adds nothing new to the theory here; his contribution is packaging it with the specific %MV numbers (see [[framework--on-field-rehab-levels-with-mv-bands]]).

**When NOT to apply** — The complexity axis as Harries operationalizes it rests on an older, information-processing model of motor learning (blocked-to-serial-to-random practice, described in Part 5; see [[framework--practice-structure-block-serial-random-by-level]]), not on ecological dynamics/representative learning design. His example of "closed reactivity" is a coach throwing a hand signal - a generic, arbitrary stimulus, not the game-relevant information a player actually reads (a defender's hips, a gap opening). He names "constraints-based learning design" once, in this same module, and never operationalizes it. In this model, complexity is switched on once intensity is judged safe; in an ecological model, representative information should be present and scaled from the start, not withheld until Level 4. This is a genuine theoretical gap, flagged here as **contested** against the library's ecological-dynamics sources, not a reason to discard the intensity/complexity distinction itself, which still holds.

**Example** — A hamstring athlete at 82% max velocity with force benchmarks not yet cleared should still run in a controlled, closed environment even if his skill work has already moved to a positional, semi-random drill; conversely, an athlete cleared on force benchmarks but still hesitant in decision-making needs complexity pushed even at a plateaued running intensity.

**Related** — [[research-papers/taberner-2022-contextual-considerations-using-the-control-chaos-continuum-for-return-to-sport-in-elite-f]] (Taberner's own control-chaos continuum, the framework Harries is built on: suggested reciprocal link, "applied and re-dosed by a Sportsmith practitioner course, see on-field-rtp--harries"); [[research-papers/taberner-2019-physical-preparation-and-return-to-sport-of-the-football-player-with-a-tibia-fibula-fractu]]; [[skill-acquisition/enhancing-skill--myszka/framework--nonlinear-pedagogy-and-constraint-classes]] and [[skill-acquisition/enhancing-skill--myszka/principle--representative-design]] (the ecological-dynamics alternative to Harries' complexity operationalization); [[framework--practice-structure-block-serial-random-by-level]]

# Competitive Exposure Is Not Optional Before Return

**What it is** — Harries states that the final stage of on-field rehab and the first return-to-training exposures must achieve both high intensity and high complexity together, and that exposing the athlete to genuinely competitive, high-pressure situations before return is "critical to successful return to play outcomes," not an optional nice-to-have. He frames the target behaviorally: the athlete must show restored ability, confidence and willingness to choose the right action in the right environment under competitive pressure, for example not hesitating to accelerate through a gap in the defense (~09:47-10:49).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: none of the locomotor actions rebuilt in isolation (running fast, cutting, decelerating) are performed in isolation during a game; they are always embedded in a competitive, time-pressured decision. If the last thing an athlete experiences before return is a controlled, cooperative drill, the first time they face real defensive pressure is in the game itself.

**When to apply** — Build the return-to-training block deliberately around live, competitive, small-sided or positional work at game-relevant intensity, not just a volume ramp of straight-line running. Treat "has he been exposed to live competitive pressure" as its own checklist item separate from "has he hit his MV and force benchmarks."

**When NOT to apply** — Harries gives no way to measure "confidence and willingness" other than by watching for hesitation, which is the exact gap this principle creates (see [[heuristic--hesitation-signals-unready-but-is-unmeasured]]). Do not treat a subjective "he looked confident" as equivalent to the objective force/velocity gates; it is a real criterion but currently an unmeasured one at Baylor, same as in Harries' own course.

**Example** — In Part 6, the athlete in [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] had his return delayed a full week specifically to add more training exposure rather than accept a physically-ready but under-exposed return; that decision reflects this principle even though it cost time.

**Related** — [[framework--intensity-complexity-two-independent-axes]]

# Hesitation Is a Named Readiness Red Flag, With No Way to Measure It

**What it is** — Harries names hesitation as a disqualifying sign: an athlete not confidently and willingly choosing the right action under competitive pressure (e.g., not accelerating through a gap) is, in his framing, not ready to return (~10:15-10:49, and see [[principle--competitive-exposure-required-before-return-to-play]]). He never gives a way to observe, score or record it.

**Why it works** — Harries offers no mechanism, only the assertion. It is plausible on its face: hesitation under pressure plausibly reflects unresolved fear-avoidance or a lack of trust in the injured tissue. But plausibility is not the same as a defined, repeatable observation.

**When to apply** — Flag it as exactly what it is: a real, named criterion the course itself cannot defend to an objective audience. It is a legitimate prompt to look for a way to operationalize "hesitation" (a success-rate threshold on a drill, a scripted-start/live-finish task design, video-coded decision latency) rather than to rely on a coach's unaided impression, but this course supplies none of those tools itself.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not write "athlete showed no hesitation" into a Baylor RTP note as if it were a measured criterion on par with the % MV or force benchmarks in [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]]. It is currently an unvalidated, single-observer judgment call with no defined pass/fail rule, exactly the kind of subjective criterion the 75-85% gate's objective benchmarks were designed to avoid relying on alone.

**Example** — Two athletes both clear their force benchmarks and %MV targets; one accelerates confidently through a small-sided game gap, the other visibly slows and checks his own leg before committing. Harries would treat the second as not ready, but the course gives no rule for how many hesitant reps, or what kind, would actually hold up a return decision.

**Related** — [[principle--competitive-exposure-required-before-return-to-play]]

# A Framework Is a Guide, Not a Protocol

**What it is** — Harries lists four reasons to build an on-field rehab framework rather than freelance each case: (1) it acts as a guardrail against progressing an athlete too fast into a negative reloading response or recurrence; (2) aligning it to the sport's actual performance requirements improves an athlete's preparedness on return; (3) it stays flexible enough to individualize the rehab, because "it can't be too rigid... a framework for me would be a guide, not a step-by-step process"; (4) it creates efficiency and consistency in programming and in-the-moment decisions, which in his experience raises trust between practitioner and athlete (~00:39-02:01).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: a framework externalizes the decision logic (what to progress, in what order, under what conditions) so decisions under time pressure are faster and more defensible, without pretending every case fits the same fixed sequence.

**When to apply** — Use this as the pitch for why Applied Performance should hand Athletic Medicine a shared decision structure (levels, gates, exit criteria) rather than case-by-case verbal negotiation each time an athlete nears return. It is also the justification for building the framework at all, before any of the specific numbers below.

**When NOT to apply** — A framework that hardens into a fixed protocol defeats its own stated purpose. If Applied Performance builds phased levels and % MV gates for Baylor, they need to stay adjustable to injury severity, athlete history, season timing and organizational culture, per Harries' own repeated point in the exit-rule discussion (see [[heuristic--two-exposures-above-90-percent-mv-exit-rule]]) that he "can't tell you whether you need one, two, or seven" exposures - that answer is context-dependent, not fixed by the framework.

**Example** — Two hamstring cases in Part 6 used the same levels and pillars but different session frequencies, interval formats and undulation patterns because of different injury histories (see [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] vs [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]]); the framework held, the prescription did not.

**Related** — [[framework--intensity-complexity-two-independent-axes]]

# The Five On-Field Rehab Levels, With Max-Velocity Bands

**What it is** — Harries splits on-field rehab into five levels, aligned to early/mid/late rehab, followed by return-to-training and return-to-play (Part 2, ~02:54-04:16). Each level targets a max-velocity (MV) band for linear running (Part 3, ~08:39-09:14; confirmed Part-3.pdf p.2):

| Level | Target % of max velocity |
|---|---|
| 1 | ~50-70% |
| 2 | ~70-75% |
| 3 | ~75-85% |
| 4 | ~85-95% |
| 5 | >95% up to 100% |

For his illustrative low-grade hamstring case, this maps to one session per level (sessions 1-5), then two return-to-training sessions (sessions 6-7) with the team, then return to play as session 8 (~03:30-04:16). He is explicit this is a minor-injury example: "with a more severe injury or different type of injury... you may do a number of sessions in each level before moving on."

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: splitting rehab into named levels gives structure to the gradual stressing of sport-specific locomotor actions, aligned to where the athlete sits in the overall rehab (gym-based early, on-field mid, transition-to-training late).

**When to apply** — Use the five-level structure as the shared vocabulary between Applied Performance and Athletic Medicine: "Level 3" means a defined, measurable thing (75-85% of *that athlete's own* MV, from the Catapult pipeline), not a vague stage description. The number of sessions per level is explicitly not fixed by the framework and should scale with injury severity and history (see [[principle--framework-is-a-guide-not-a-protocol]]).

**When NOT to apply** — The MV bands are Harries' own teaching example and expert-opinion breakpoints, not derived from trial data; he presents no evidence citation for why the boundaries sit at exactly 70/75/85/95%. They are AFL-cohort numbers (based on GPS-derived %MV for the sport). Football's per-position sprint demands are different from AFL's continuous locomotor profile, so the level *structure* (five stages, submax-to-max) transfers, but the specific %MV/km-h breakpoints should be checked against Baylor's own GPS data per position before being treated as a Baylor standard, and Baylor's data dictionary does not yet have position-specific thresholds built (`method-baseline.md`, Load monitoring and GPS section notes this as unfinished work).

**Example** — See [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]] for a real (non-illustrative) case where this level structure was applied but the athlete never reached the desired >90% exposure due to external season-timing pressure - the levels held, the ideal endpoint did not.

**Related** — [[framework--invasion-sport-locomotor-pillars]]; [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]] (the criteria for crossing Level 2 into Level 3); [[heuristic--two-exposures-above-90-percent-mv-exit-rule]] (the Level 5 exit criterion)

# Speed Gains Shift From Ankle-Dominant to Hip-Dominant

**What it is** — Harries claims that the mechanism by which an athlete increases running speed changes as speed rises. From slow jogging to moderate running speeds (~6-7 m/s), speed is gained mainly by increasing stride length, which he calls "typically an ankle-dominant strategy." Once an athlete reaches moderate speeds where a striding pattern emerges, further speed increases come mainly from increasing stride frequency, which he calls "typically a more hip-dominant strategy" (~02:35-03:19). He states this has direct rehab implications: tailor drill selection toward ankle-loading tasks for calf/Achilles/ankle injuries at lower speeds, and toward hip-loading tasks for hip-region injuries as speed approaches striding/sprinting.

**Why it works** — No mechanism or citation is given beyond the assertion itself; it reads as an established coaching heuristic in sprint biomechanics circles (stride length increases dominate early acceleration, stride frequency and ground-contact mechanics dominate near top speed) but Harries presents it as fact without evidence.

**When to apply** — Use it as a reason to sequence drill emphasis by injury site: for an ankle/Achilles/calf injury, prioritize competency in the lower-speed, longer-ground-contact, ankle-loaded phases (jogging, running) before pushing toward striding; for a hip-region injury (adductor, proximal hamstring), be more cautious as speed approaches the striding-to-sprinting transition where hip-dominant, higher-frequency mechanics take over.

**When NOT to apply** — This is stated as fact, not tested against Baylor's own case data or cited to a specific biomechanics source in the course, and the ankle/hip split is almost certainly an oversimplification: sprint mechanics research shows both joints contribute throughout, with relative contribution shifting gradually rather than switching at a discrete speed. Do not use this as a precise cutoff for clearing an athlete to a given speed based on which joint "took over"; use it only as a soft prioritization heuristic, and verify any specific injury-tailoring decision against the athlete's own force-plate and Nordic/Iso Seated Calf data rather than this claim alone.

**Example** — A returning athlete with an Achilles repair would spend more deliberate time in ankle-loaded dribble/A-skip preparatory drills (see [[framework--running-prep-drill-menu]]) before advancing toward the striding-pattern band (~75-85% MV) where hip-dominant mechanics become more prominent, per this claim.

**Related** — [[framework--running-gait-speed-categories]]; [[framework--running-prep-drill-menu]]

# Running Preparation Drill Menu (Pre-Running to Level 1)

**What it is** — Before an athlete returns to actual running, Harries prescribes a menu of low-intensity drills to re-familiarize the athlete with upright-running postures and prepare tissue for repetitive loading (~03:41-08:03; confirmed Part-3.pdf p.2):
- **Dribble walks/runs** over ankle, shin and knee height - front-side mechanics focus, flat foot contact, "nothing goes out the back."
- **Dribble transitions** between ankle/shin/knee heights over 5 m segments, transitioning into a typical running gait.
- **Skipping variations**, e.g. A-skips, to add stiffness and reactivity on ground contact.
- **Low-intensity jumping**: pogos and unilateral pogos, for repetitive loading-cycle and system-stiffness preparation.
- **Scissor shuffles and scissor bounds**: aggressive hip flexion/extension, striking under center of mass, building horizontal displacement.

Basic clinical criteria (appropriate range of motion, minimal pain/swelling, sufficient local endurance/strength) plus a demonstrated ability to produce force quickly in a dynamic task and tolerate repetitive impact are the prerequisites before commencing actual running; often this is judged functionally (can they do these drills without issue) rather than via a formal test (~07:43-08:28).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: these drills rebuild the specific postures, coordination and ground-contact stiffness of upright running at low tissue stress before loading the same patterns at running speed, and build the athlete's confidence in the injured area.

**When to apply** — Use as the standard Level-1/pre-running menu for any lower-limb soft-tissue RTP at Baylor. Because these are low intensity, they can also stay in the warm-up throughout later on-field rehab levels, not just at the start (~07:32-07:43).

**When NOT to apply** — This is a generic menu, not tailored by injury site beyond the general logic in [[claim--ankle-then-hip-dominant-speed-mechanism]] (e.g., dribble drills over knee height load the hip flexors more than ankle-height dribbles). Do not treat "completed the drill menu" as a substitute for the actual clinical criteria (ROM, pain, strength) it is meant to sit alongside; the drills demonstrate functional tolerance, they do not replace a clinical assessment.

**Example** — Harries' hamstring case study begins on-field rehab with this drill menu before any timed running, confirming the athlete can tolerate repetitive ground contact and produce force dynamically before session 1's 60 m repeats begin (see [[heuristic--fixed-distance-timed-repeats-for-pacing]]).

**Related** — [[claim--ankle-then-hip-dominant-speed-mechanism]]; [[framework--on-field-rehab-levels-with-mv-bands]]

# Broken-Stride Timing: Time Only the Middle Phase

**What it is** — Once an athlete progresses beyond ~70-75% of MV, Harries moves from full-distance timed repeats to a "broken stride": a run divided into an acceleration phase, a speed-maintenance phase and a deceleration phase, e.g. 60 m split into 20 m / 20 m / 20 m (adjustable, e.g. 15/10/15 to demand a more aggressive acceleration into the same target speed) (~17:01-18:20). Critically, he times only the middle (speed-maintenance) phase, not the whole distance, because that isolates the actual target speed from the acceleration and deceleration mechanics around it. Worked example: hitting 2.88-3.0 seconds across the middle phase equates to ~24-25 km/h, which is ~70-75% of that athlete's MV (~18:29-18:51); the next progression steps require 2.77-2.88 seconds through the same phase, pushing speed up roughly 1 km/h more. He prefers a stopwatch for immediate feedback, using GPS/video as a secondary confirmation of peak velocity, not the primary control method (~18:51-19:17).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: timing the whole distance conflates three different physical demands (accelerating, holding speed, decelerating) into one number, so it can't precisely control what speed was actually reached in the middle. Isolating and timing only the maintenance phase gives a direct, controllable readout of the target velocity, and lets the acceleration/deceleration phase lengths be manipulated independently to change the aggressiveness of the accel or decel without changing the target maintenance speed.

**When to apply** — Use for on-field rehab levels roughly 2 through 5, once an athlete is working above ~70-75% MV, as the standard method for prescribing and verifying max-velocity exposures. At later levels, continue shortening the acceleration-phase distance (while keeping the target maintenance speed) to increase acceleration magnitude, and build in fatiguing conditions before high-%MV maintenance-phase reps.

**When NOT to apply** — Harries explicitly becomes "far less rigid" with these time targets in later rehab stages, adding a percentage-bandwidth range instead of a single time, because forcing a fixed time can push an athlete faster than they are comfortable with or unnecessarily hold them back; he pairs each rep with a conversation (how did that feel, are you comfortable) rather than treating the stopwatch number as absolute (~20:17-20:48). Do not apply this as a rigid pass/fail number in late-stage rehab without that check-in.

**Example** — See [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]] for the objective criteria Harries applies before letting an athlete progress past the 70-75% zone this protocol is designed to hit precisely.

**Related** — [[heuristic--fixed-distance-timed-repeats-for-pacing]]; [[framework--repeat-sprint-interval-format-under-fatigue]]

# The 75-85% Max-Velocity Gate

**What it is** — Before progressing an athlete past roughly 75-85% of MV (Harries states the gate at "75-85%" in most places and once as "75-80%," ~13:04-16:35; the broken-stride worked example itself targets 70-75%, a step below the gate, not the gate threshold), Harries checks four things (~13:31-15:45, confirmed Part-3.pdf p.3):
1. **Time for biological healing** appropriate to the injury.

# At Least One, Ideally Two, Exposures Above 90% MV Before Return

**What it is** — Harries' exit rule for on-field rehab: before returning an athlete to training or play, he wants at least one, ideally two, exposures above 90% of MV (~23:24-24:41). He is explicit there is no universal number: "I can't tell you whether you need to do one, two, or seven. That's entirely dependent on the injury... your organisational culture, your philosophy at your club... the history of that player and their soft tissue history... the pressure in that time of year." The one firm line he draws: he cannot imagine returning an athlete to training, and certainly not to play, without at least one, probably two, exposures above 90%.

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: exposures near true maximal velocity load the tissue in a way that submaximal running does not rehearse, so returning without ever having approached game-realistic top speed leaves an unrehearsed gap between rehab and competition, regardless of how much submaximal volume was accumulated.

**When to apply** — Use as a floor, not a target: before clearing a returning athlete, confirm at least one (preferably two) session exposures above 90% of that athlete's own MV have been logged and tolerated without a negative symptom response. Track exposures explicitly per athlete rather than assuming volume accumulated lower down the intensity scale is an adequate substitute.

**When NOT to apply** — This is expert opinion/common practice, not a validated cutoff, and Harries' own four case studies show it is routinely not met: [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]] returned with zero exposures above 90% (external season-timing pressure); [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]] returned with only one, when Harries "would have preferred a second." Do not treat missing this exit rule as an automatic hold on return; it is one input among the injury history, schedule and organizational context he lists, and both of his under-target cases returned to play regardless. Also do not assume "90% of max velocity" is the same absolute speed across sports or positions; it must be computed from the athlete's own MV, and Baylor's own GPS/max-velocity pipeline (Catapult/OpenField) is the source for that number, not a generic AFL threshold.

**Example** — [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] is the opposite case: because that athlete's low running frequency meant every late session ran near-maximal, he accumulated six separate exposures above 90% MV before return, far more than the stated floor, illustrating that the number is a byproduct of the chosen periodization, not a targeted count.

**Related** — [[framework--on-field-rehab-levels-with-mv-bands]]; [[heuristic--linear-then-undulating-mv-progression]]

# Progress Max Velocity Linearly, Then Undulate Near 80-85%

**What it is** — Harries' default periodization for max-velocity exposure across sessions: increase speed session-on-session in a linear fashion through the early-to-mid part of rehab, then shift to an undulating pattern (down, up, sometimes down and back up to hold a level) once the athlete approaches roughly 80-85% of MV (~21:17-22:50; confirmed Part-3.pdf p.3). His illustrative hamstring case goes linear through session 5 (50-60% -> 65-70% -> 75-80% -> 85% -> ~90-92% of MV), pushed further into the linear zone than typical (up to 90-92%) because of time pressure toward a 3-4 week return, then brings intensity down before the next jump.

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: linear progression is appropriate early because the tissue is far from its ceiling and each step is a modest incremental stress; near 80-85% MV, sessions get close enough to true maximal effort that repeating high-intensity exposures session after session risks accumulating fatigue and reload risk faster than the tissue can adapt, so alternating higher and lower sessions manages that fatigue while still working toward more >90% exposures over time.

**When to apply** — Use linear progression as the default through on-field rehab levels 1-3 (up to ~75-85% MV), then switch to an undulating high/low pattern from roughly level 3-4 onward. How long to stay linear (and how far past 85% to push before undulating) is explicitly context-dependent on time pressure, injury severity and history, not fixed.

**When NOT to apply** — Not every case in Harries' own material follows this pattern: [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] used a flat, non-undulating linear build because the low running frequency (twice weekly) meant every session was already spaced far enough apart to serve as its own recovery; forcing an undulating pattern onto a low-frequency case would be unnecessary. Do not apply the linear-then-undulate default mechanically without checking whether session frequency already provides the recovery spacing undulation is meant to create.

**Example** — Contrast [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]] and [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]] (both undulated from around session 6) against [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] (stayed linear throughout, by design).

**Related** — [[heuristic--two-exposures-above-90-percent-mv-exit-rule]]

# Broken-Stride Timing: Time Only the Middle Phase

**What it is** — Once an athlete progresses beyond ~70-75% of MV, Harries moves from full-distance timed repeats to a "broken stride": a run divided into an acceleration phase, a speed-maintenance phase and a deceleration phase, e.g. 60 m split into 20 m / 20 m / 20 m (adjustable, e.g. 15/10/15 to demand a more aggressive acceleration into the same target speed) (~17:01-18:20). Critically, he times only the middle (speed-maintenance) phase, not the whole distance, because that isolates the actual target speed from the acceleration and deceleration mechanics around it. Worked example: hitting 2.88-3.0 seconds across the middle phase equates to ~24-25 km/h, which is ~70-75% of that athlete's MV (~18:29-18:51); the next progression steps require 2.77-2.88 seconds through the same phase, pushing speed up roughly 1 km/h more. He prefers a stopwatch for immediate feedback, using GPS/video as a secondary confirmation of peak velocity, not the primary control method (~18:51-19:17).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: timing the whole distance conflates three different physical demands (accelerating, holding speed, decelerating) into one number, so it can't precisely control what speed was actually reached in the middle. Isolating and timing only the maintenance phase gives a direct, controllable readout of the target velocity, and lets the acceleration/deceleration phase lengths be manipulated independently to change the aggressiveness of the accel or decel without changing the target maintenance speed.

**When to apply** — Use for on-field rehab levels roughly 2 through 5, once an athlete is working above ~70-75% MV, as the standard method for prescribing and verifying max-velocity exposures. At later levels, continue shortening the acceleration-phase distance (while keeping the target maintenance speed) to increase acceleration magnitude, and build in fatiguing conditions before high-%MV maintenance-phase reps.

**When NOT to apply** — Harries explicitly becomes "far less rigid" with these time targets in later rehab stages, adding a percentage-bandwidth range instead of a single time, because forcing a fixed time can push an athlete faster than they are comfortable with or unnecessarily hold them back; he pairs each rep with a conversation (how did that feel, are you comfortable) rather than treating the stopwatch number as absolute (~20:17-20:48). Do not apply this as a rigid pass/fail number in late-stage rehab without that check-in.

**Example** — See [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]] for the objective criteria Harries applies before letting an athlete progress past the 70-75% zone this protocol is designed to hit precisely.

**When NOT to apply** — This is expert opinion/common practice, not a validated cutoff, and Harries' own four case studies show it is routinely not met: [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]] returned with zero exposures above 90% (external season-timing pressure); [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]] returned with only one, when Harries "would have preferred a second." Do not treat missing this exit rule as an automatic hold on return; it is one input among the injury history, schedule and organizational context he lists, and both of his under-target cases returned to play regardless. Also do not assume "90% of max velocity" is the same absolute speed across sports or positions; it must be computed from the athlete's own MV, and Baylor's own GPS/max-velocity pipeline (Catapult/OpenField) is the source for that number, not a generic AFL threshold.

**Example** — [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] is the opposite case: because that athlete's low running frequency meant every late session ran near-maximal, he accumulated six separate exposures above 90% MV before return, far more than the stated floor, illustrating that the number is a byproduct of the chosen periodization, not a targeted count.

# Progress Max Velocity Linearly, Then Undulate Near 80-85%

**What it is** — Harries' default periodization for max-velocity exposure across sessions: increase speed session-on-session in a linear fashion through the early-to-mid part of rehab, then shift to an undulating pattern (down, up, sometimes down and back up to hold a level) once the athlete approaches roughly 80-85% of MV (~21:17-22:50; confirmed Part-3.pdf p.3). His illustrative hamstring case goes linear through session 5 (50-60% -> 65-70% -> 75-80% -> 85% -> ~90-92% of MV), pushed further into the linear zone than typical (up to 90-92%) because of time pressure toward a 3-4 week return, then brings intensity down before the next jump.

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: linear progression is appropriate early because the tissue is far from its ceiling and each step is a modest incremental stress; near 80-85% MV, sessions get close enough to true maximal effort that repeating high-intensity exposures session after session risks accumulating fatigue and reload risk faster than the tissue can adapt, so alternating higher and lower sessions manages that fatigue while still working toward more >90% exposures over time.

**When to apply** — Use linear progression as the default through on-field rehab levels 1-3 (up to ~75-85% MV), then switch to an undulating high/low pattern from roughly level 3-4 onward. How long to stay linear (and how far past 85% to push before undulating) is explicitly context-dependent on time pressure, injury severity and history, not fixed.

**When NOT to apply** — Not every case in Harries' own material follows this pattern: [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] used a flat, non-undulating linear build because the low running frequency (twice weekly) meant every session was already spaced far enough apart to serve as its own recovery; forcing an undulating pattern onto a low-frequency case would be unnecessary. Do not apply the linear-then-undulate default mechanically without checking whether session frequency already provides the recovery spacing undulation is meant to create.

**Example** — Contrast [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]] and [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]] (both undulated from around session 6) against [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] (stayed linear throughout, by design).
