# Eight Intensity Levers for Multidirectional Speed and Agility

**What it is** — Harries names the dials that manipulate the intensity of acceleration, deceleration and change-of-direction (COD) work. Part 4 gives six mechanical/environmental levers explicitly (~04:54-06:52; confirmed cleanly in Part-4.pdf p.2): **velocity change magnitude** (bigger accel/decel = higher force), **entry velocity** (higher approach speed raises eccentric braking demand into a decel or COD), **COD angle** (sharper cuts, e.g. 135-180 degrees, load the plant/penultimate step harder than shallow ones and raise knee joint loading), **preparation distance/time** (more distance/time to prepare allows multiple foot contacts to dissipate braking force across steps; less time raises knee valgus moment on side-step cuts), **space available** (smaller spaces constrain approach velocity), and **reactivity** (pre-planned/closed vs. open/evasive). Two further, more perceptual continuums are layered on top: **% effort** (a self-regulated prescribed effort cap, e.g. "70-75% effort today") and **% of max velocity**, giving eight total levers. In Part 6's case-study review, he re-frames this as "four main levers" (rate of velocity change, entry velocity, COD angle, and decision time/anticipation), primarily adjusted via three channels: perceived effort/intensity, space, and reactivity (~11:39-12:26) - the same set of factors, described at a coarser grain for retrospective case analysis.

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: these are the mechanical and perceptual variables that actually determine how physically and cognitively demanding a cutting/accel/decel task is, so naming them turns "make this drill harder" from a feel-based judgment into an explicit, adjustable checklist.

**When to apply** — Use this as the input schema for designing or auditing any acceleration/deceleration/COD drill in on-field rehab: state which levers are set high or low, rather than describing a drill only by its name. It is the single most reusable table in the course for building a drill-design tool or checklist.

**When NOT to apply** — The levers do not operate independently (see [[principle--intensity-levers-interact-not-independent]]); do not treat them as separately tunable dials without checking cross-effects. The "reactivity" lever is also the course's weakest link theoretically - see [[heuristic--closed-vs-open-reactivity-drill-design]] for why "closed reactivity" as Harries defines it is not the same as game-representative information.

**Example** — See [[framework--mdsa-drill-menu-by-level]] for how these levers map onto concrete drills across on-field rehab levels 1-5.

**Related** — [[research-papers/young-2022-agility-in-invasion-sports-position-stand-of-the-iusca]] (the peer-reviewed position stand on the multidirectional-speed/agility split Harries uses informally; suggested reciprocal link: "a practitioner course's intensity-lever operationalization of this position stand's speed/agility distinction, see on-field-rtp--harries"); [[framework--intensity-complexity-drill-plotting-tool]]

# The Intensity Levers Interact, They Don't Adjust Independently

**What it is** — Harries stresses that the eight (or four, coarser-grain) intensity levers for multidirectional speed and agility work "don't operate independently... changing one factor can actually have an impact on another factor." His examples: raising the magnitude of acceleration (velocity-change lever) forces a higher entry velocity into the following decel/COD; shrinking the available space constrains approach velocity, which in turn lowers the intensity of a cut even as it raises the drill's complexity (~07:45-08:29, ~09:47-10:11).

**Why it works** — The levers describe one interconnected physical system (an athlete's momentum and the space/time they have to change it), not eight separate knobs; pulling one necessarily moves at least one other, so treating them as independent will produce drills whose actual difficulty doesn't match what was intended.

**When to apply** — When designing or auditing a drill, always ask which other levers a given change will move, not just the one being adjusted. Use this explicitly to explain the counterintuitive case: shrinking a grid's size can *lower* the intensity of a cut (because it caps entry velocity) while simultaneously *raising* its complexity (because it now demands tighter spatial and decision-making precision) - intensity and complexity moving in opposite directions from the same manipulation.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not use this as an excuse to avoid the intensity/complexity plotting exercise in [[framework--intensity-complexity-drill-plotting-tool]]; the interactions are real but the plotting tool is specifically designed to let a practitioner reason about the net effect after accounting for them, rather than being defeated by the complexity of tracking every lever separately.

**Example** — A 3x3 m diamond-drill grid used at low intensity in early on-field rehab (see [[framework--mdsa-drill-menu-by-level]]) constrains approach velocity by space alone, which is why it can safely be introduced early even though lateral shuffling and direction changes are technically "COD" work.

**Related** — [[framework--eight-intensity-levers-mdsa]]

# Plot Drills on an Intensity x Complexity Chart to Build a Drill Menu

**What it is** — Harries' method for turning the intensity-lever list into a usable drill library: draw a chart with intensity on the vertical axis and complexity on the horizontal axis, then place individual drills on it using judgment about where their constraints put them. He gives a worked example: does adding a ball-dribbling task to a curvilinear sprint move it down the complexity axis? If so, move the drill accordingly (~09:07-10:18; confirmed Part-4.pdf p.2-3: "Drills can be plotted on a matrix of intensity (vertical axis) and complexity (horizontal axis). Early rehab drills sit low on both, while later-stage drills push into high intensity and high complexity."). Once a set of drills is plotted, they naturally cluster into which on-field rehab level they belong to, and the same exercise applies to sport-specific skill drills, not just MDSA drills (Part 5).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: this operationalizes the abstract intensity/complexity distinction from [[framework--intensity-complexity-two-independent-axes]] into a concrete design tool - instead of guessing which level a drill belongs in, you place it by explicitly reasoning through its constraints on both axes.

**When to apply** — Use this as the design method for building a Baylor-specific drill library (per level, per pillar): rather than copying Harries' AFL drill menu directly, run each candidate drill (including a proposed contact/collision drill for football) through this same plotting exercise using Baylor's own constraint vocabulary.

**When NOT to apply** — This tool depends on practitioner judgment for where a drill sits on each axis; it produces a defensible visual, not an objectively validated coordinate. Do not treat the resulting chart placement as more precise than the judgment calls that produced it.

**Example** — [[framework--mdsa-drill-menu-by-level]] is the output of running this exercise for Harries' own case-study drills.

**Related** — [[framework--eight-intensity-levers-mdsa]]; [[framework--intensity-complexity-two-independent-axes]]

# Multidirectional Speed & Agility Drill Menu by On-Field Rehab Level

**What it is** — Harries' worked drill menu for the hamstring case study, by level (~11:56-21:11; confirmed Part-4.pdf p.3):
- **Levels 1-2** (low intensity, low complexity, block practice): fast-easy-fast accelerations (accelerate ~5 m, ease off, re-accelerate); go-and-stop accelerations (accelerate a set distance, brake to a stop in a deceleration zone); curvy-linear ("half bend") accelerations; 30-degree cutting gates with a pre-planned side step, crossover step, or split step; a 3x3 m diamond/square drill with athlete-chosen lateral/forward/backward shuffling.
- **Level 3** (rising velocity/space, controlled/closed reactivity introduced): fast-easy-fast acceleration with a closed-reactive defender (defender moves laterally to open space); a defensive reaction (mirror) drill in a small square; a "compass drill" with pre-determined or reactive 45/90/135-degree direction changes at ~75-80% effort, cued by a hand signal.
- **Level 4** (near-maximal velocity ~80-85%, bigger spaces, more open reactivity): partner chase-and-tag; a large-space gate drill with a turnover cue requiring a hard deceleration and chase; a reactive compass drill in a bigger space followed by a second reactive task (react to a rolled ball).
- **Level 5** (highly chaotic, near-maximal/maximal): sport-specific, competitive, multi-athlete scenarios; where extra players/coaches aren't available, use constrained drills designed to replicate unpredictability as closely as possible.

**Why it works** — Each level's drills are the concrete output of running the levers in [[framework--eight-intensity-levers-mdsa]] through the plotting exercise in [[framework--intensity-complexity-drill-plotting-tool]]: space shrinks or grows, reactivity moves from none to closed to open, and entry velocity/COD angle both rise, in a sequence matched to the level's target physical readiness.

**When to apply** — Use this menu as a starting drill bank for building a Baylor-specific version; the drill *shapes* (accelerate-then-react, gated cutting, chase-and-tag, compass drill) transfer across sports even where the specific angles or spaces would be adjusted for football positions.

**When NOT to apply** — This is one practitioner's AFL menu, built for an athlete with no contact restriction; none of these drills involve or prepare for a blocking, tackling or hand-fighting demand, so a football-specific menu needs an added contact-drill category this course does not supply (see [[framework--invasion-sport-locomotor-pillars]]). The "reactivity" drills here are also limited to hand signals and mirrored defenders, not genuine game-representative cues (see [[heuristic--closed-vs-open-reactivity-drill-design]]).

**Example** — In [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]], sessions 3, 5 and 8 map closely onto this Level 1-3 / Level 3-4 / Level 4-5 menu progression.

**Related** — [[framework--eight-intensity-levers-mdsa]]; [[heuristic--closed-vs-open-reactivity-drill-design]]

# Closed, Then Open, Then Evasive Reactivity

**What it is** — Harries' reactivity ladder for progressing drill unpredictability: pre-planned (fully known in advance) -> closed reactivity (a single, simple cue ends the drill, e.g. a coach throwing a hand signal to cue a cut) -> open reactivity (a further task follows the first reaction, cued by a noise, another athlete, or a coach) -> evasive/competitive (genuinely live, opposed play) (~15:45-16:06, ~17:51-18:12, ~20:34-20:58).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: unpredictability should be added gradually, matched to the athlete's readiness, rather than jumping straight from fully controlled to fully live play.

**When to apply** — Use the four-step ladder shape (planned -> closed -> open -> evasive) as the ordering principle for adding reactivity to any drill, matched to the on-field rehab level.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested.** Harries' worked examples of "closed reactivity" are a coach's arbitrary hand signal or a defender mirroring a shuffle - a generic stimulus with no game meaning, not the information a player actually reads in competition (a defender's hip position, a gap opening in coverage). This is the course's clearest departure from an ecological-dynamics view of skill acquisition, which holds that the information source should be representative of the game from the start (a real defender's movement, not an arbitrary cue) and scaled in difficulty, rather than substituted with an arbitrary cue early and only made representative once complexity is judged "safe." Read ecologically, Harries' own four rungs re-map to: unopposed -> still unopposed (an arbitrary cue is not opposition) -> partly opposed -> opposed. Do not treat "closed reactivity" drills as teaching a player anything about reading a real opponent; they add unpredictability of *timing*, not unpredictability of *information*.

**Example** — The compass drill in [[framework--mdsa-drill-menu-by-level]] (Level 3) uses a coach's hand signal to cue a direction change - closed reactivity by Harries' definition, but not representative of what a defender's body actually signals in a game.

# Eight Intensity Levers for Multidirectional Speed and Agility

**What it is** — Harries names the dials that manipulate the intensity of acceleration, deceleration and change-of-direction (COD) work. Part 4 gives six mechanical/environmental levers explicitly (~04:54-06:52; confirmed cleanly in Part-4.pdf p.2): **velocity change magnitude** (bigger accel/decel = higher force), **entry velocity** (higher approach speed raises eccentric braking demand into a decel or COD), **COD angle** (sharper cuts, e.g. 135-180 degrees, load the plant/penultimate step harder than shallow ones and raise knee joint loading), **preparation distance/time** (more distance/time to prepare allows multiple foot contacts to dissipate braking force across steps; less time raises knee valgus moment on side-step cuts), **space available** (smaller spaces constrain approach velocity), and **reactivity** (pre-planned/closed vs. open/evasive). Two further, more perceptual continuums are layered on top: **% effort** (a self-regulated prescribed effort cap, e.g. "70-75% effort today") and **% of max velocity**, giving eight total levers. In Part 6's case-study review, he re-frames this as "four main levers" (rate of velocity change, entry velocity, COD angle, and decision time/anticipation), primarily adjusted via three channels: perceived effort/intensity, space, and reactivity (~11:39-12:26) - the same set of factors, described at a coarser grain for retrospective case analysis.

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: these are the mechanical and perceptual variables that actually determine how physically and cognitively demanding a cutting/accel/decel task is, so naming them turns "make this drill harder" from a feel-based judgment into an explicit, adjustable checklist.

**When to apply** — Use this as the input schema for designing or auditing any acceleration/deceleration/COD drill in on-field rehab: state which levers are set high or low, rather than describing a drill only by its name. It is the single most reusable table in the course for building a drill-design tool or checklist.

**When NOT to apply** — The levers do not operate independently (see [[principle--intensity-levers-interact-not-independent]]); do not treat them as separately tunable dials without checking cross-effects. The "reactivity" lever is also the course's weakest link theoretically - see [[heuristic--closed-vs-open-reactivity-drill-design]] for why "closed reactivity" as Harries defines it is not the same as game-representative information.

**Example** — See [[framework--mdsa-drill-menu-by-level]] for how these levers map onto concrete drills across on-field rehab levels 1-5.

**Related** — [[research-papers/young-2022-agility-in-invasion-sports-position-stand-of-the-iusca]] (the peer-reviewed position stand on the multidirectional-speed/agility split Harries uses informally; suggested reciprocal link: "a practitioner course's intensity-lever operationalization of this position stand's speed/agility distinction, see on-field-rtp--harries"); [[framework--intensity-complexity-drill-plotting-tool]]

# The Intensity Levers Interact, They Don't Adjust Independently

**What it is** — Harries stresses that the eight (or four, coarser-grain) intensity levers for multidirectional speed and agility work "don't operate independently... changing one factor can actually have an impact on another factor." His examples: raising the magnitude of acceleration (velocity-change lever) forces a higher entry velocity into the following decel/COD; shrinking the available space constrains approach velocity, which in turn lowers the intensity of a cut even as it raises the drill's complexity (~07:45-08:29, ~09:47-10:11).

**Why it works** — The levers describe one interconnected physical system (an athlete's momentum and the space/time they have to change it), not eight separate knobs; pulling one necessarily moves at least one other, so treating them as independent will produce drills whose actual difficulty doesn't match what was intended.

**When to apply** — When designing or auditing a drill, always ask which other levers a given change will move, not just the one being adjusted. Use this explicitly to explain the counterintuitive case: shrinking a grid's size can *lower* the intensity of a cut (because it caps entry velocity) while simultaneously *raising* its complexity (because it now demands tighter spatial and decision-making precision) - intensity and complexity moving in opposite directions from the same manipulation.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not use this as an excuse to avoid the intensity/complexity plotting exercise in [[framework--intensity-complexity-drill-plotting-tool]]; the interactions are real but the plotting tool is specifically designed to let a practitioner reason about the net effect after accounting for them, rather than being defeated by the complexity of tracking every lever separately.

**Example** — A 3x3 m diamond-drill grid used at low intensity in early on-field rehab (see [[framework--mdsa-drill-menu-by-level]]) constrains approach velocity by space alone, which is why it can safely be introduced early even though lateral shuffling and direction changes are technically "COD" work.

**Related** — [[framework--eight-intensity-levers-mdsa]]

**What it is** — Harries' method for turning the intensity-lever list into a usable drill library: draw a chart with intensity on the vertical axis and complexity on the horizontal axis, then place individual drills on it using judgment about where their constraints put them. If so, move the drill accordingly (~09:07-10:18; confirmed Part-4.pdf p.2-3: "Drills can be plotted on a matrix of intensity (vertical axis) and complexity (horizontal axis). Early rehab drills sit low on both, while later-stage drills push into high intensity and high complexity."). Once a set of drills is plotted, they naturally cluster into which on-field rehab level they belong to, and the same exercise applies to sport-specific skill drills, not just MDSA drills (Part 5).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: this operationalizes the abstract intensity/complexity distinction from [[framework--intensity-complexity-two-independent-axes]] into a concrete design tool - instead of guessing which level a drill belongs in, you place it by explicitly reasoning through its constraints on both axes.

**When to apply** — Use this as the design method for building a Baylor-specific drill library (per level, per pillar): rather than copying Harries' AFL drill menu directly, run each candidate drill (including a proposed contact/collision drill for football) through this same plotting exercise using Baylor's own constraint vocabulary.

**When NOT to apply** — This tool depends on practitioner judgment for where a drill sits on each axis; it produces a defensible visual, not an objectively validated coordinate. Do not treat the resulting chart placement as more precise than the judgment calls that produced it.

**Example** — [[framework--mdsa-drill-menu-by-level]] is the output of running this exercise for Harries' own case-study drills.

# Block, Then Serial, Then Random Practice Across the Levels

**What it is** — Harries maps sport-specific skill drills onto a practice-structure continuum borrowed from motor-learning theory: **block practice** (the same drill repeated, low variability), **serial practice** (a known sequence of actions, predictable order), and **random practice** (unpredictable, variable order/decisions). He assigns these across levels (~04:03-07:26, confirmed Part-5.pdf p.2): Level 1 - solely block, tightly controlled; Level 2 - still block, intensity of the drills rises; Level 3 - roughly 50/50 block and serial, chaining action sequences; Level 4 - block dropped entirely, mostly serial with some random; Level 5 - substantial random practice, with some serial retained deliberately for actions not yet ready for full unpredictability. On return to training, levels 1-2 of training itself are "pretty much all" random.

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: block-to-serial-to-random is a graded route from fully predictable to fully unpredictable practice, which lets an athlete build a skill under low cognitive/decision load first and only add decision-making demand once the movement itself is competent.

**When to apply** — Use the general shape (predictable early, unpredictable late) as the practice-structure axis alongside drill type and movement level (see [[framework--sport-skill-drill-type-continuum-by-level]]) when designing sport-specific skill sessions.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested.** Block/serial/random and its associated "contextual interference effect" come from the Schmidt information-processing tradition of motor learning, not from ecological dynamics/representative learning design, which the library's skill-acquisition sources treat as the better-supported model for sport skill transfer. The practical difference matters: under an information-processing view, predictability itself is the variable being controlled, and the task's informational content is secondary; under an ecological view, the key variable is whether the *information* driving the action is representative of the game (a real defender, a real developing gap) regardless of how "predictable" the drill's structure is. A block-practice drill against a live, representative defender can be more transferable than a "random" drill built on arbitrary, non-representative cues. Do not assume moving along this block-serial-random axis is equivalent to moving toward game transfer; check whether the *information* in the drill, not just its unpredictability, is representative.

# Withhold Sport Skills by Which Structure They Load, Not by Level Alone

**What it is** — Harries tailors sport-specific skill drills to the specific injured structure, not just to the generic level number. In his hamstring case: at Level 1, kicking is withheld entirely on the injured limb (only the uninjured limb performs stationary technical actions); at Level 2, kicking is reintroduced on the injured limb but kept stationary and pre-planned (~08:16-08:33, ~00:00:08 continued). The general logic: identify which specific technical action loads the injured tissue, and progress that action's introduction on its own timeline distinct from the general level progression.

**Why it works** — A generic level-based progression ("Level 2 = some movement") would not by itself capture that kicking loads the hamstring specifically; withholding by structure adds a second, injury-specific axis to the generic drill-type continuum in [[framework--sport-skill-drill-type-continuum-by-level]].

**When to apply** — For any RTP case, identify up front which specific sport skills load the injured structure (kicking for a hamstring/hip flexor; throwing for a shoulder/elbow; blocking or a three-point stance for a knee or ankle) and build a separate withhold-then-reintroduce timeline for that specific action, layered on top of the general level progression.

**When NOT to apply** — This only works cleanly when a skill action can be isolated to one limb or structure. Bilateral or trunk-driven skills (a quarterback's throwing motion after a core or oblique strain, a lineman's stance after a hip injury) don't decompose this cleanly into "injured-limb version withheld, uninjured-limb version allowed," so the isolation logic needs to be rebuilt case-by-case rather than assumed.

**Example** — A returning kicker/punter with a hamstring strain would follow this exact logic: full participation in every other technical/tactical drill from Level 1, but kicking itself withheld until Level 2 and only reintroduced stationary at first.

**Related** — [[framework--sport-skill-drill-type-continuum-by-level]]

# Case Study: Proximal Hamstring Strain, Grade 2 (Case 1)

**What it is** — Grade 2 strain at the musculotendinous junction of biceps femoris and semitendinosus, acute non-contact running mechanism, AFL. Return to play (RTP) day 28: six rehab-running sessions, three partial-training sessions, two full-training sessions (~01:53-02:18, ~04:18-05:04). Days 0-5 off legs (isometrics, low-intensity eccentrics, general strength, running-prep drills); first run day 6; running sessions days 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 17; modified training day 19; full training day 25; RTP day 28.

**Max velocity progression.** Sessions 1-2: basic running-mechanics drills, jog-walk intervals at 8-12 km/h, then 100 m repeats at a time-based pace averaging ~16-20 km/h. Sessions 3-4: 60 m repeats progressing 13 s down to 10.5 s (18-22.5 km/h target). Session 5: strides with an acceleration/maintenance/deceleration structure targeting 70-85% MV. Session 8: continued strides plus higher-intensity flies at 85-92% MV. From session 6 onward, periodization shifted from linear to undulating. **The athlete did not reach above 90% MV before returning to play** - Harries attributes this to external pressure (approaching finals), calling it "an example of... a tension here between the ideal programming and some of the contextual demands" (~06:48-07:09).

**HSR/VHSR/sprint volumes.** Speed thresholds for this dataset: high-speed running (HSR) >17 km/h, very-high-speed running (VHSR) >23 km/h, sprint >27 km/h (~85% max for these athletes) (~09:57-10:17). VHSR peaked at 86% of game value by day 21 ("slightly lower than desired, but still okay"). Sprint-zone exposure was under-dosed: Harries states he wanted closer to 50-60% of game demands and did not get the drill design and execution right to hit it (~10:53-11:04; this passage is somewhat garbled in the transcript and should not be conflated with Case 2's separate 40%-of-game-volume under-dose at its own session 7).

**Multidirectional speed/agility (MDSA).** Session 3: introductory curvilinear/S-bend runs, forward/backward ladders, non-reactive diamond drills (low intensity, fully planned). Session 5: fast-easy-fast accelerations, go-and-stop drills, a closed-reactive compass drill (45-135 degrees at ~75-80% effort), a defensive reaction (mirror) drill. # Case Study: Semimembranosus Strain With Adductor Magnus Involvement (Case 2)

**What it is** — Grade 2 strain, classified as "`[classification name unclear]` 2B, proximal hamstring strain with a longitudinal tendon split" (the classification system name is unclear in the audio near ~02:24 and is left unresolved here), acute non-contact running mechanism, AFL. RTP day 30: six rehab-running sessions, two modified-training sessions, three full-training sessions. **The athlete returned to play one week earlier than the medical/performance team's own recommendation** - Harries flags this explicitly as "the real world nature of decision making" (~02:36-02:46).

**Max velocity progression.** Days 0-4 off legs; two non-consecutive running exposures week 1 (days 5, 7); three non-consecutive sessions week 2, increasing intensity/volume. Sessions 1-5: linear increase (mechanics drills, time-based 100 m repeats, then faster 60 m repeats, then strides, then flies). Sessions 6-8: undulating pattern. **Two exposures above 90% MV were achieved before return**: day 22 at 96.7% and day 27 at 92.1% - Harries calls this "a strong application of progressive loading." Session 5 is stated to be functionally identical to Case 1's session 5 (60 m reps building 18-22.5 km/h, then six strides: two at 70-75%, two at 75-80%, two at ~82.5% MV, effort-based and GPS-confirmed), which he says typifies a mid-rehab max-velocity checkpoint around day 10-14 post-injury, with ~85% MV treated as a sound ceiling until force-production and reactive-strength criteria are confirmed. Session 8 (coinciding with return to full training): progressive 60 m strides, three 20 m flies at 85-95% MV, and **repeat sprint intervals**: two sets of three to four reps over 40 m, all above 85% MV, on a 30-second rolling start (rep 1 at 0 s, rep 2 at 30 s, rep 3 at 60 s) - see [[framework--repeat-sprint-interval-format-under-fatigue]].

**HSR/VHSR/sprint volumes.** Same thresholds as Case 1 (17/23/27 km/h). Session 2 produced an unexpected HSR overshoot via 100 m repeats; Harries notes this matters less here because 17 km/h is only ~55-60% of max for these athletes (see [[heuristic--low-speed-threshold-inflates-hsr-totals]]). From session 3, HSR delivered via short-interval formats (10 s on/10 s off, 20 s on/20 s off); from session 8, small-sided games contributed HSR organically. VHSR/sprint built linearly sessions 4-8, but **session 7/day 19 under-dosed at only 40% of game volume** (Harries wanted 70-80%); session 8 then peaked at 120% of game value.

**MDSA.** Sessions 2-3: basic curvilinear runs, linear/lateral shuffling. Session 4: low-velocity cutting, basic accel/decel drills. Sessions 5-6: velocity change graded up, closed reactivity (visual/verbal cues) added. Session 7: higher entry/change velocities, larger spaces, still closed-reactive. Session 8: evasive drills at lower velocities in smaller spaces (deliberately lower isolated-MDSA volume that session, offset by a fortunate scheduling window - the reserves team's bye gave more athletes for higher-quality skill-drill exposure instead). Session 9 onward: high-velocity evasive MDSA in realistic/competitive contexts.

**Sport-specific skill.** Sessions 2-3: low-load stationary handball/short kicking. Sessions 3-4: controlled movement added to technical execution. Sessions 5-6: positional-specific drills with movement fatigue. Sessions 7-8: small-group competitive play (3v3, 5v5 handball). Week 4: large-group competitive play in the main training session before return.

**Why it works** — This case shows the framework producing a well-dosed sprint exposure (two exposures >90% MV, repeat-sprint intervals for fatigue-state sprinting) even while the actual return date was moved up by organizational decision-making outside the physical-readiness plan.

**When to apply** — Use as the reference case for "physical readiness criteria met or exceeded, but the actual return decision still overridden by other factors" - a reminder that meeting the framework's numbers does not by itself control the return-to-play date.

**When NOT to apply** — n=1, retrospective, self-reported; the one-week-early return is presented as a fact of what happened, not validated as safe by any outcome data beyond it being reported without a stated recurrence.

**Example** — See [[framework--repeat-sprint-interval-format-under-fatigue]] for the reusable session-design pattern this case's session 8 exemplifies.

**Related** — [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]]; [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]]

# Case Study: Recurrent Lateral Soleus Strain, Grade 2 (Case 3)

**What it is** — Grade 2 recurrent lateral soleus strain, acute non-contact running incident, AFL. RTP day 44: five rehab-running sessions, one partial-training session, three full-training sessions. **Return to play was deliberately delayed a further week** by the medical/performance team specifically to add training exposure (~26:59-27:28). Twelve days off legs (longer than Cases 1-2); running resumed day 13 after two low-intensity running-prep sessions (days 9, 11). From that point, **running occurred only twice per week** with at least 48 hours (sometimes 72-96 hours) between sessions - a deliberate low-frequency strategy because this athlete had responded well to reduced running frequency in the past, and reduced frequency/weekly load has worked for the club's other recurrent calf injuries (~27:59-28:33).

**Max velocity progression.** Familiar stages (mechanics, 60 m repeats, strides, flies), but periodization was distinct: the first four sessions built linearly, then **from session 4 onward the athlete consistently exceeded 90% MV in every remaining session** - a flat, non-undulating pattern, which Harries attributes simply to the low running frequency giving each session enough inherent recovery spacing. The athlete accumulated **six separate exposures above 90% MV before return - the most of any of the four cases** (~29:03-29:37). Session 1 deliberately used low volume and long recoveries to minimize localized calf fatigue: 60 m repeats limited to four reps per set every 45 seconds, then a couple of 100 m repeats at four reps per set every 60 seconds. Session 4 transitioned to higher intensity: progressive 60 m repeats, 60 m strides, and a single 60 m fly at 88-93% MV. The return-to-sport-phase session (~session 7) used two 60 m strides in the warm-up, three 60 m fly runs building to peak effort, and **one set** (not two, unlike Case 2) of three to four 40 m repeat sprints above 85% MV on a 30-second turnaround.

**HSR/VHSR/sprint volumes.** Sessions 1-3 deliberately held HSR very low (30-40% of match load) and did not progress it, specifically to protect the calf from cumulative loading. Interval durations followed a **short-to-long model** (60 m repeats first, progressing to longer 100 m repeats and 40-60 s intervals) - the opposite sequencing from the hamstring cases' long-to-short approach (see [[heuristic--short-to-long-vs-long-to-short-intervals-by-injury]]). Between sessions 7-9, HSR exposure was deliberately *reduced* to prioritize mechanical (accel/decel/COD) and sport-specific loads instead, once the extended timeline had already banked enough HSR volume. VHSR/sprint built linearly sessions 3-8, reaching 75% of game values on days 30 and 38 (Harries would have preferred 85-100% for more robust preparation).

**MDSA and sport-skill.** Because of the reduced running frequency, "each session entailed a suitable progression" on its own (session = progression step), rather than being spread across many sessions: sessions 2-3 change-of-direction introduction, session 4 low-velocity cutting/accel/decel, session 5 moderate velocity change with closed reactivity (the athlete placed only in the offensive role, matching his real game role), session 6 higher entry velocities and evasion in smaller spaces, sessions 7-9 high-velocity evasive MDSA fully integrated into live team training (no isolated MDSA work needed by session 7). Sport skill followed the standard stationary -> movement -> positional/fatigue -> competitive-play progression, with three high-quality full-training sessions carrying complex tactical demands before return.

**Why it works** — This case demonstrates the framework's structure (levels, intensity/complexity progression) holding while the actual periodization (frequency, undulation, interval length sequencing) was substantially rebuilt around one specific, recurring-injury constraint: minimizing cumulative local fatigue to the calf.

**When to apply** — Use as the template for adapting session frequency and interval sequencing for a *recurrent* soft-tissue injury, not just a first-time strain - see [[heuristic--reduce-frequency-for-recurrent-calf-injury]].

**When NOT to apply** — n=1, retrospective, self-reported. This is also the case with the most conservative constraint (recurrence) and the most extended timeline; its specific frequency/interval choices should not be generalized to a first-time strain of the same tissue.

# Case Study: Grade 3 MCL Sprain With Meniscal Involvement (Case 4)

**What it is** — Grade 3 MCL sprain with a posterior meniscal tear, direct contact mechanism, AFL - the only contact-mechanism, and only joint (rather than muscle-tendon), case of the four. RTP day 49: eight rehab-running sessions, one partial-training session, four full-training sessions. The athlete was **braced for the first three to four weeks**, and the first run (day 17) was performed in the brace, after indoor running-prep sessions (low-intensity ankle-dominant jumps, dribbles over ankles, A-skips) (~36:52-37:18). Weeks 3-4: three non-consecutive running sessions per week. Week 5: running frequency deliberately reduced to two larger-load sessions to bridge into a bigger planned session at the end of week 6 (a match-load-comparable rehab session preparing for a week 7 return). Week 7: small session early, moderate midweek (matching the team's normal in-season schedule), RTP at week's end.

**Max velocity progression.** Classic linear-then-undulating pattern (as in Cases 1-2): sessions 1-7/8 built linearly; sessions 9-13 onward undulated high-intensity exposures against recovery. **Only one exposure above 90% MV was achieved before return** - Harries says he would have preferred a second, on day 47, but for an unspecified reason the athlete did not hit it that day; he calls the single exposure "conservative" (~38:52-39:07). Example sessions: session 3 - dribbles/mechanics, then two sets of eight 100 m repeats (set 1 at 14-16 km/h, set 2 at 16-18 km/h). Session 5 (still early rehab) - three sets of 400 m repeats progressing speed each set, then two to three 60 m strides at 70-75% - "the first exposure to higher intensity running." Session 7 (levels 4-5) - 60 m strides progressing 70% to 85%, then two 60 m fly runs at 85-88%. Session 10 (return-to-sport phase) - warm-up strides at 70-80%, two 60 m flies at 88-93%, plus one set of the standard 40 m repeat-sprint format under fatigue.

**Straight-line-only constraint and its inconsistency in the source.** Because this was a knee-joint injury requiring brace time, change-of-direction (COD) work was deliberately delayed. The transcript states this constraint two different ways at different points: "sessions one to six was straight line running only" (~41:15-41:22) and, describing MDSA specifically, "sessions one to four, we had no change direction whatsoever" with low-intensity COD introduced starting session 5 (~42:30-43:08). # Case Study: Proximal Hamstring Strain, Grade 2 (Case 1)

**What it is** — Grade 2 strain at the musculotendinous junction of biceps femoris and semitendinosus, acute non-contact running mechanism, AFL. Return to play (RTP) day 28: six rehab-running sessions, three partial-training sessions, two full-training sessions (~01:53-02:18, ~04:18-05:04). Days 0-5 off legs (isometrics, low-intensity eccentrics, general strength, running-prep drills); first run day 6; running sessions days 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 17; modified training day 19; full training day 25; RTP day 28.

**Max velocity progression.** Sessions 1-2: basic running-mechanics drills, jog-walk intervals at 8-12 km/h, then 100 m repeats at a time-based pace averaging ~16-20 km/h. Sessions 3-4: 60 m repeats progressing 13 s down to 10.5 s (18-22.5 km/h target). Session 5: strides with an acceleration/maintenance/deceleration structure targeting 70-85% MV. Session 8: continued strides plus higher-intensity flies at 85-92% MV. From session 6 onward, periodization shifted from linear to undulating. **The athlete did not reach above 90% MV before returning to play** - Harries attributes this to external pressure (approaching finals), calling it "an example of... a tension here between the ideal programming and some of the contextual demands" (~06:48-07:09).

**HSR/VHSR/sprint volumes.** Speed thresholds for this dataset: high-speed running (HSR) >17 km/h, very-high-speed running (VHSR) >23 km/h, sprint >27 km/h (~85% max for these athletes) (~09:57-10:17). VHSR peaked at 86% of game value by day 21 ("slightly lower than desired, but still okay"). Sprint-zone exposure was under-dosed: Harries states he wanted closer to 50-60% of game demands and did not get the drill design and execution right to hit it (~10:53-11:04; this passage is somewhat garbled in the transcript and should not be conflated with Case 2's separate 40%-of-game-volume under-dose at its own session 7).

**Multidirectional speed/agility (MDSA).** Session 3: introductory curvilinear/S-bend runs, forward/backward ladders, non-reactive diamond drills (low intensity, fully planned). Session 5: fast-easy-fast accelerations, go-and-stop drills, a closed-reactive compass drill (45-135 degrees at ~75-80% effort), a defensive reaction (mirror) drill. Session 8: higher-velocity crossover cuts and Z-runs at 85-90% effort, extended compass drills (added evasive movement after the cut), 2v1 attacking squares (small to large), modified handball games with obstacles (3v2, three x two-minute efforts with two-minute recovery). From session 10, MDSA was delivered mainly through sport-specific/competitive drills.

**Sport-specific skill.** Sessions 3-5: low-intensity technical actions (stationary kicking/handball), then controlled movement. From session 6: positional-specific drills under fatigue (volume/technical output under load). Sessions 8-10: competitive play in modified small-sided formats (3v2 handball), increasing decision-making demand. Full training at session 10 included large-group competitive play under near-match conditions.

**When NOT to apply** — This is n=1, retrospective and self-reported by the practitioner who ran it; there is no outcome data here beyond "returned to play," no re-injury follow-up window reported, and no independent verification of the %MV or %game-value figures. **What it is** — Grade 2 strain, classified as "`[classification name unclear]` 2B, proximal hamstring strain with a longitudinal tendon split" (the classification system name is unclear in the audio near ~02:24 and is left unresolved here), acute non-contact running mechanism, AFL. **Max velocity progression.** Days 0-4 off legs; two non-consecutive running exposures week 1 (days 5, 7); three non-consecutive sessions week 2, increasing intensity/volume. Sessions 1-5: linear increase (mechanics drills, time-based 100 m repeats, then faster 60 m repeats, then strides, then flies). Sessions 6-8: undulating pattern. **Two exposures above 90% MV were achieved before return**: day 22 at 96.7% and day 27 at 92.1% - Harries calls this "a strong application of progressive loading." Session 5 is stated to be functionally identical to Case 1's session 5 (60 m reps building 18-22.5 km/h, then six strides: two at 70-75%, two at 75-80%, two at ~82.5% MV, effort-based and GPS-confirmed), which he says typifies a mid-rehab max-velocity checkpoint around day 10-14 post-injury, with ~85% MV treated as a sound ceiling until force-production and reactive-strength criteria are confirmed. Session 8 (coinciding with return to full training): progressive 60 m strides, three 20 m flies at 85-95% MV, and **repeat sprint intervals**: two sets of three to four reps over 40 m, all above 85% MV, on a 30-second rolling start (rep 1 at 0 s, rep 2 at 30 s, rep 3 at 60 s) - see [[framework--repeat-sprint-interval-format-under-fatigue]].

**HSR/VHSR/sprint volumes.** Same thresholds as Case 1 (17/23/27 km/h). Session 2 produced an unexpected HSR overshoot via 100 m repeats; Harries notes this matters less here because 17 km/h is only ~55-60% of max for these athletes (see [[heuristic--low-speed-threshold-inflates-hsr-totals]]). From session 3, HSR delivered via short-interval formats (10 s on/10 s off, 20 s on/20 s off); from session 8, small-sided games contributed HSR organically. VHSR/sprint built linearly sessions 4-8, but **session 7/day 19 under-dosed at only 40% of game volume** (Harries wanted 70-80%); session 8 then peaked at 120% of game value.

**MDSA.** Sessions 2-3: basic curvilinear runs, linear/lateral shuffling. Session 4: low-velocity cutting, basic accel/decel drills. Sessions 5-6: velocity change graded up, closed reactivity (visual/verbal cues) added. Session 7: higher entry/change velocities, larger spaces, still closed-reactive. Session 8: evasive drills at lower velocities in smaller spaces (deliberately lower isolated-MDSA volume that session, offset by a fortunate scheduling window - the reserves team's bye gave more athletes for higher-quality skill-drill exposure instead). Session 9 onward: high-velocity evasive MDSA in realistic/competitive contexts.

**Sport-specific skill.** Sessions 2-3: low-load stationary handball/short kicking. Sessions 3-4: controlled movement added to technical execution. Sessions 5-6: positional-specific drills with movement fatigue. Sessions 7-8: small-group competitive play (3v3, 5v5 handball). **When NOT to apply** — n=1, retrospective, self-reported; the one-week-early return is presented as a fact of what happened, not validated as safe by any outcome data beyond it being reported without a stated recurrence.

# Case Study: Recurrent Lateral Soleus Strain, Grade 2 (Case 3)

**What it is** — Grade 2 recurrent lateral soleus strain, acute non-contact running incident, AFL. RTP day 44: five rehab-running sessions, one partial-training session, three full-training sessions. **Return to play was deliberately delayed a further week** by the medical/performance team specifically to add training exposure (~26:59-27:28). Twelve days off legs (longer than Cases 1-2); running resumed day 13 after two low-intensity running-prep sessions (days 9, 11). From that point, **running occurred only twice per week** with at least 48 hours (sometimes 72-96 hours) between sessions - a deliberate low-frequency strategy because this athlete had responded well to reduced running frequency in the past, and reduced frequency/weekly load has worked for the club's other recurrent calf injuries (~27:59-28:33).

**Max velocity progression.** Familiar stages (mechanics, 60 m repeats, strides, flies), but periodization was distinct: the first four sessions built linearly, then **from session 4 onward the athlete consistently exceeded 90% MV in every remaining session** - a flat, non-undulating pattern, which Harries attributes simply to the low running frequency giving each session enough inherent recovery spacing. The athlete accumulated **six separate exposures above 90% MV before return - the most of any of the four cases** (~29:03-29:37). Session 1 deliberately used low volume and long recoveries to minimize localized calf fatigue: 60 m repeats limited to four reps per set every 45 seconds, then a couple of 100 m repeats at four reps per set every 60 seconds. Session 4 transitioned to higher intensity: progressive 60 m repeats, 60 m strides, and a single 60 m fly at 88-93% MV. The return-to-sport-phase session (~session 7) used two 60 m strides in the warm-up, three 60 m fly runs building to peak effort, and **one set** (not two, unlike Case 2) of three to four 40 m repeat sprints above 85% MV on a 30-second turnaround.

**HSR/VHSR/sprint volumes.** Sessions 1-3 deliberately held HSR very low (30-40% of match load) and did not progress it, specifically to protect the calf from cumulative loading. Interval durations followed a **short-to-long model** (60 m repeats first, progressing to longer 100 m repeats and 40-60 s intervals) - the opposite sequencing from the hamstring cases' long-to-short approach (see [[heuristic--short-to-long-vs-long-to-short-intervals-by-injury]]). Between sessions 7-9, HSR exposure was deliberately *reduced* to prioritize mechanical (accel/decel/COD) and sport-specific loads instead, once the extended timeline had already banked enough HSR volume. VHSR/sprint built linearly sessions 3-8, reaching 75% of game values on days 30 and 38 (Harries would have preferred 85-100% for more robust preparation).

**MDSA and sport-skill.** Because of the reduced running frequency, "each session entailed a suitable progression" on its own (session = progression step), rather than being spread across many sessions: sessions 2-3 change-of-direction introduction, session 4 low-velocity cutting/accel/decel, session 5 moderate velocity change with closed reactivity (the athlete placed only in the offensive role, matching his real game role), session 6 higher entry velocities and evasion in smaller spaces, sessions 7-9 high-velocity evasive MDSA fully integrated into live team training (no isolated MDSA work needed by session 7). Sport skill followed the standard stationary -> movement -> positional/fatigue -> competitive-play progression, with three high-quality full-training sessions carrying complex tactical demands before return.

**Why it works** — This case demonstrates the framework's structure (levels, intensity/complexity progression) holding while the actual periodization (frequency, undulation, interval length sequencing) was substantially rebuilt around one specific, recurring-injury constraint: minimizing cumulative local fatigue to the calf.

**When to apply** — Use as the template for adapting session frequency and interval sequencing for a *recurrent* soft-tissue injury, not just a first-time strain - see [[heuristic--reduce-frequency-for-recurrent-calf-injury]].

**When NOT to apply** — n=1, retrospective, self-reported. This is also the case with the most conservative constraint (recurrence) and the most extended timeline; its specific frequency/interval choices should not be generalized to a first-time strain of the same tissue.

**Related** — [[heuristic--reduce-frequency-for-recurrent-calf-injury]]; [[heuristic--short-to-long-vs-long-to-short-intervals-by-injury]]; [[heuristic--linear-then-undulating-mv-progression]] (this case is the exception to that default)

# Repeat-Sprint Interval Format for Late-Stage Fatigue Exposure

**What it is** — In the back half of late-rehab sessions, Harries introduces repeat-sprint intervals to expose the athlete to high velocity under fatigue and simulate conditioning demand alongside sprint load. The format, used across three of the four case studies: **1-2 sets of three to four repetitions over 40 m, all above 85% MV, on a 30-second rolling start** (rep 1 at 0 s, rep 2 at 30 s, rep 3 at 60 s, etc.). Case 2 used **two sets**; Cases 3 and 4 used **one set** (~21:23-21:59, ~30:49-30:58, ~40:14-40:23).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: placing these in the back half of the session, after other running/skill work has already introduced some fatigue, "blends" high-speed exposure with a controlled recovery interval, giving both a sprint-load-accumulation stimulus and a conditioning stimulus at once, and rehearses producing near-maximal velocity in a fatigued state closer to what a game actually demands late in a match.

**When to apply** — Use in the return-to-sport-phase session(s), once an athlete has already cleared the 75-85% MV gate and is accumulating >90% MV exposures elsewhere in the session (see [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]] and [[heuristic--two-exposures-above-90-percent-mv-exit-rule]]). Scale the number of sets (one vs two) to the athlete's overall session load and injury type - the lower-frequency recurrent-calf case ([[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]]) used only one set.

**When NOT to apply** — This is placed deliberately late in rehab, after force-production benchmarks are already cleared; it should not be used as an early-rehab or pre-gate exposure, since it combines near-maximal velocity with accumulated fatigue, precisely the combination the earlier gate criteria are designed to screen for readiness against.

**Example** — See [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]] session 8 for the two-set version and [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]] session 10 for the one-set version used alongside a knee-joint injury.

# Sequence Interval Length by Which Tissue Is Injured

**What it is** — Across the four case studies, Harries used two different interval-length sequencing strategies depending on injury type. The hamstring cases ([[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]], [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]]) more commonly used a **long-to-short** approach (starting with longer repeats, e.g. 100 m, and moving toward shorter, faster efforts). The recurrent calf case ([[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]]) deliberately used the opposite, a **short-to-long** model: beginning with 60 m repeats (10-12 s efforts) and progressing to longer intervals (100 m repeats at 20-24 s, then 40 s and 60 s intervals), explicitly to control the calf's cumulative local-fatigue exposure early (~31:41-32:04).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: the calf contributes disproportionately to running mechanics at all speeds (not just top speed), so short, well-spaced efforts early minimize repetitive local loading to the injured structure while still allowing systemic running-mechanics practice; longer intervals are then added once tolerance is established. For the hamstring, which is loaded more specifically during the late-swing phase at higher speeds, starting with longer, moderate-pace efforts and shortening toward faster, more targeted reps was the pattern used instead, though he does not spell out an equivalent explicit rationale for the hamstring ordering.

**When to apply** — When designing early on-field rehab running volume, consider the injured tissue's loading profile (does it load more with repetition frequency, as with calf, or more with peak intensity, as with hamstring at high speed) and choose interval length progression accordingly, rather than defaulting to one fixed sequencing rule for every lower-limb injury.

**When NOT to apply** — This is drawn from only two data points (one calf case, two hamstring cases) inside one practitioner's own case selection; Harries never states it as a general rule, and this entry infers the generalization from the pattern across his four cases. Treat it as a hypothesis worth testing against Baylor's own case data, not an established principle.

**Example** — Contrast [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]]'s 60m-then-100m-then-longer intervals against [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]]'s and [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]]'s early use of 100 m repeats before moving to faster 60 m work.

# Cut Running Frequency for a Recurrent Calf Injury

**What it is** — For a recurrent lateral soleus strain, Harries deliberately ran the athlete only **twice per week**, with at least 48 hours (sometimes 72-96 hours) between sessions, instead of the more frequent running used in the hamstring cases. His stated reasons: this specific athlete had responded well to reduced running frequency after past calf issues, and reduced frequency/weekly load "has also been effective in some of our recurrent calf injuries that we've come across in the past" at his organization (~27:59-28:33, ~29:53-30:01).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: lower frequency gives the calf longer recovery windows between loading bouts, which matters more for a muscle that is loaded on effectively every ground contact (unlike, say, a hamstring loaded mainly in late swing at higher speeds) and which had already re-injured once under a more standard frequency.

**When to apply** — For a recurrent (not first-time) calf/soleus strain, consider deliberately lower running frequency (e.g., twice weekly with 48+ hour gaps) as a starting strategy, especially if the athlete has a documented history of responding well to reduced frequency previously.

**When NOT to apply** — This is based on organizational pattern-matching and one athlete's own history ("he had responded well... in the past"), not a controlled comparison; it is explicitly *not* what Harries did for the hamstring cases, so do not port this frequency reduction to hamstring or other tissue types without the same recurrence-and-prior-response rationale. It also extended this athlete's total time loss to 44 days (the longest of the four cases, deliberately extended a further week for training exposure), a real cost that should be weighed against the injury-recurrence risk it aims to reduce.

**Example** — See [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] for the full case; contrast with [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]]'s six sessions across roughly the same number of weeks as this case's five sessions across a longer span.

# A Low High-Speed-Running Threshold Can Inflate Totals

**What it is** — Harries' organization set high-speed running (HSR) at >17 km/h, very-high-speed running (VHSR) at >23 km/h, and sprint at >27 km/h, and he notes 17 km/h is only roughly 55-60% of max velocity for these AFL athletes (~10:57-11:04, repeated ~22:54-23:11). Because the HSR cutoff sits at a relatively low %MV, a rep or drill that only briefly crosses it can register as a full HSR exposure and inflate the session or weekly total, even though the athlete never approached a meaningful intensity. This happened twice in his four cases: an unexpected HSR overshoot in [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]] session 2 (100 m repeats), and an unplanned overshoot in [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]] session 4.

**Why it works** — A fixed absolute speed threshold (km/h) captures a different %MV for every athlete and, within one athlete, becomes an easier bar to clear (relatively) than a %MV-based threshold would be, so longer-distance reps or drills with any build-up phase are especially prone to briefly crossing a low absolute cutoff without the practitioner intending a high-speed exposure.

**When to apply** — When reviewing GPS load reports, check where the HSR/VHSR/sprint speed cutoffs sit relative to the individual athlete's own %MV, not just the absolute km/h number; a rep or session total should be read alongside how much of it came from brief threshold crossings versus sustained high-intensity running. This is the specific point Baylor's own gap analysis should address (see When NOT to apply).

**When NOT to apply** — Do not assume these AFL-specific thresholds (17/23/27 km/h) apply to Baylor football; Baylor's own documented data dictionary is currently generic and vendor-organized rather than sport- or position-specific (`method-baseline.md`, Load monitoring and GPS section), so equivalent thresholds need to be derived from Baylor's own Catapult/OpenField data per position, not imported from this AFL cohort. A football lineman, for instance, may rarely or never reach a comparable sprint-zone speed in a game at all, which would make an imported absolute threshold meaningless for that position without being re-checked against Baylor's own data first.

**Example** — See [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]] session 4: the athlete gained confidence running in the brace and accumulated HSR via a mix of 100 m repeats and three-minute intervals, overshooting the plan - flagged by Harries as low-risk precisely because the threshold crossed was such a low %MV for that athlete.

**Related** — [[principle--percent-of-game-value-as-volume-metric]]

# 17 km/h ≈ 55-60% MV, 27 km/h ≈ 85% MV, For This AFL Cohort

**What it is** — Harries states the organization's fixed GPS speed-zone cutoffs converted, for these athletes, to roughly: high-speed running threshold (17 km/h) ≈ 55-60% of max velocity; sprint threshold (27 km/h) ≈ 85% of max velocity "for most of our athletes at that club" (~09:57-10:17, ~22:54-23:11). Very-high-speed running (23 km/h) sits between the two, roughly 70% MV by the same logic, though he does not state that conversion explicitly.

**Why it works** — This is a cohort-average conversion, presented as an observed fact about this specific group of AFL athletes' typical max velocities relative to the club's fixed absolute speed zones, not a derived or universal formula.

**When to apply** — Use as a worked example of *how* to convert an absolute GPS speed threshold into a %MV figure for a given population, and as the reason a fixed km/h threshold behaves differently across athletes with different MVs (see [[heuristic--low-speed-threshold-inflates-hsr-totals]]).

**When NOT to apply** — This conversion is specific to Harries' AFL cohort's own average max velocities; it should not be applied to Baylor football athletes, whose MV distribution (and therefore the %MV a given km/h threshold represents) will differ by sport and very likely by position. Baylor's own speed-zone thresholds are not yet position-specific (`method-baseline.md`), so the correct move is to compute the equivalent conversion from Baylor's own Catapult MV data per player or position group, not to reuse these percentages.

**Example** — A Baylor GPS threshold set generically at, say, 16 km/h for "high-speed running" would represent a very different %MV for a 30 km/h-MV wide receiver than for a 24 km/h-MV offensive lineman; this claim is the reminder to check that conversion per player/position rather than assume it.

# Track Running Volume as a Percent of the Athlete's Own Game Value

**What it is** — Rather than reporting HSR/VHSR/sprint volumes as raw meters, Harries tracks and reports them as a **percent of that athlete's own game-average value** for the metric, session by session: e.g. "VHSR peaked at 86% of game value by day 21," "sprint exposure... maybe around 50-60% of game demands," "session 8 peaked at 120% of game value" (Case 1 and 2, throughout Part 6). Game demand benchmarks are established from the athlete's own historical GPS data (Part 1's case-study demographic: ~13 km total distance, ~1000 m HSR, ~200 m VHSR, 40-50 accels/decels per game, 34.2 km/h MV) (~02:20-02:49).

**Why it works** — An absolute meters figure means nothing without a denominator; normalizing to "% of what this specific athlete actually does in a game" makes progress legible across the whole rehab (is this session under-, on-, or over-dosed relative to competition) and comparable across sessions and cases despite different absolute demands per position or per athlete.

**When to apply** — Build every RTP running report at Baylor around this same normalization: compute each returning athlete's own game-average HSR/VHSR/sprint/accel-decel numbers from their historical Catapult data, then report every rehab session as a % of that individual baseline, not as a raw distance. This directly operationalizes the review's stated first-ship recommendation (a Baylor velocity-band sheet reporting exactly this line per player).

**When NOT to apply** — This metric is only as good as the game-average baseline it's normalized against; a baseline built from too few games, an unrepresentative sample (e.g., mostly blowout or short-rotation games), or the wrong position comparison will distort every subsequent % figure. It is also an AFL-cohort practice built on a continuous, high-running sport; Baylor football is intermittent and position-specific, so the same %-of-game-value logic transfers, but the underlying km/h zone definitions and accel/decel counts have to be re-derived per position from Baylor's own GPS, not copied from AFL norms (many linemen, for instance, may rarely or never reach a comparable sprint-zone speed in a game at all, which would make a raw %-of-game-value sprint figure close to meaningless for that position without checking the baseline first).

**Example** — See [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]], where the same session (session 8) simultaneously showed a 120%-of-game-value peak in VHSR/sprint alongside a lower isolated-MDSA volume - both numbers only interpretable relative to that athlete's own game baseline.

# Repeat-Sprint Interval Format for Late-Stage Fatigue Exposure

**What it is** — In the back half of late-rehab sessions, Harries introduces repeat-sprint intervals to expose the athlete to high velocity under fatigue and simulate conditioning demand alongside sprint load. The format, used across three of the four case studies: **1-2 sets of three to four repetitions over 40 m, all above 85% MV, on a 30-second rolling start** (rep 1 at 0 s, rep 2 at 30 s, rep 3 at 60 s, etc.). Case 2 used **two sets**; Cases 3 and 4 used **one set** (~21:23-21:59, ~30:49-30:58, ~40:14-40:23).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: placing these in the back half of the session, after other running/skill work has already introduced some fatigue, "blends" high-speed exposure with a controlled recovery interval, giving both a sprint-load-accumulation stimulus and a conditioning stimulus at once, and rehearses producing near-maximal velocity in a fatigued state closer to what a game actually demands late in a match.

**When to apply** — Use in the return-to-sport-phase session(s), once an athlete has already cleared the 75-85% MV gate and is accumulating >90% MV exposures elsewhere in the session (see [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]] and [[heuristic--two-exposures-above-90-percent-mv-exit-rule]]). **When NOT to apply** — This is placed deliberately late in rehab, after force-production benchmarks are already cleared; it should not be used as an early-rehab or pre-gate exposure, since it combines near-maximal velocity with accumulated fatigue, precisely the combination the earlier gate criteria are designed to screen for readiness against.

**Example** — See [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]] session 8 for the two-set version and [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]] session 10 for the one-set version used alongside a knee-joint injury.

# Sequence Interval Length by Which Tissue Is Injured

**What it is** — Across the four case studies, Harries used two different interval-length sequencing strategies depending on injury type. The hamstring cases ([[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]], [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]]) more commonly used a **long-to-short** approach (starting with longer repeats, e.g. 100 m, and moving toward shorter, faster efforts). The recurrent calf case ([[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]]) deliberately used the opposite, a **short-to-long** model: beginning with 60 m repeats (10-12 s efforts) and progressing to longer intervals (100 m repeats at 20-24 s, then 40 s and 60 s intervals), explicitly to control the calf's cumulative local-fatigue exposure early (~31:41-32:04).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: the calf contributes disproportionately to running mechanics at all speeds (not just top speed), so short, well-spaced efforts early minimize repetitive local loading to the injured structure while still allowing systemic running-mechanics practice; longer intervals are then added once tolerance is established. For the hamstring, which is loaded more specifically during the late-swing phase at higher speeds, starting with longer, moderate-pace efforts and shortening toward faster, more targeted reps was the pattern used instead, though he does not spell out an equivalent explicit rationale for the hamstring ordering.

**When to apply** — When designing early on-field rehab running volume, consider the injured tissue's loading profile (does it load more with repetition frequency, as with calf, or more with peak intensity, as with hamstring at high speed) and choose interval length progression accordingly, rather than defaulting to one fixed sequencing rule for every lower-limb injury.

**When NOT to apply** — This is drawn from only two data points (one calf case, two hamstring cases) inside one practitioner's own case selection; Harries never states it as a general rule, and this entry infers the generalization from the pattern across his four cases. Treat it as a hypothesis worth testing against Baylor's own case data, not an established principle.

**Example** — Contrast [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]]'s 60m-then-100m-then-longer intervals against [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]]'s and [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]]'s early use of 100 m repeats before moving to faster 60 m work.

**Related** — [[heuristic--reduce-frequency-for-recurrent-calf-injury]]

# Cut Running Frequency for a Recurrent Calf Injury

**What it is** — For a recurrent lateral soleus strain, Harries deliberately ran the athlete only **twice per week**, with at least 48 hours (sometimes 72-96 hours) between sessions, instead of the more frequent running used in the hamstring cases. His stated reasons: this specific athlete had responded well to reduced running frequency after past calf issues, and reduced frequency/weekly load "has also been effective in some of our recurrent calf injuries that we've come across in the past" at his organization (~27:59-28:33, ~29:53-30:01).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: lower frequency gives the calf longer recovery windows between loading bouts, which matters more for a muscle that is loaded on effectively every ground contact (unlike, say, a hamstring loaded mainly in late swing at higher speeds) and which had already re-injured once under a more standard frequency.

**When to apply** — For a recurrent (not first-time) calf/soleus strain, consider deliberately lower running frequency (e.g., twice weekly with 48+ hour gaps) as a starting strategy, especially if the athlete has a documented history of responding well to reduced frequency previously.

**When NOT to apply** — This is based on organizational pattern-matching and one athlete's own history ("he had responded well... in the past"), not a controlled comparison; it is explicitly *not* what Harries did for the hamstring cases, so do not port this frequency reduction to hamstring or other tissue types without the same recurrence-and-prior-response rationale. It also extended this athlete's total time loss to 44 days (the longest of the four cases, deliberately extended a further week for training exposure), a real cost that should be weighed against the injury-recurrence risk it aims to reduce.

**Example** — See [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] for the full case; contrast with [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]]'s six sessions across roughly the same number of weeks as this case's five sessions across a longer span.

# A Low High-Speed-Running Threshold Can Inflate Totals

**What it is** — Harries' organization set high-speed running (HSR) at >17 km/h, very-high-speed running (VHSR) at >23 km/h, and sprint at >27 km/h, and he notes 17 km/h is only roughly 55-60% of max velocity for these AFL athletes (~10:57-11:04, repeated ~22:54-23:11). Because the HSR cutoff sits at a relatively low %MV, a rep or drill that only briefly crosses it can register as a full HSR exposure and inflate the session or weekly total, even though the athlete never approached a meaningful intensity. This happened twice in his four cases: an unexpected HSR overshoot in [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]] session 2 (100 m repeats), and an unplanned overshoot in [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]] session 4.

**Why it works** — A fixed absolute speed threshold (km/h) captures a different %MV for every athlete and, within one athlete, becomes an easier bar to clear (relatively) than a %MV-based threshold would be, so longer-distance reps or drills with any build-up phase are especially prone to briefly crossing a low absolute cutoff without the practitioner intending a high-speed exposure.

**When to apply** — When reviewing GPS load reports, check where the HSR/VHSR/sprint speed cutoffs sit relative to the individual athlete's own %MV, not just the absolute km/h number; a rep or session total should be read alongside how much of it came from brief threshold crossings versus sustained high-intensity running. This is the specific point Baylor's own gap analysis should address (see When NOT to apply).

**When NOT to apply** — Do not assume these AFL-specific thresholds (17/23/27 km/h) apply to Baylor football; Baylor's own documented data dictionary is currently generic and vendor-organized rather than sport- or position-specific (`method-baseline.md`, Load monitoring and GPS section), so equivalent thresholds need to be derived from Baylor's own Catapult/OpenField data per position, not imported from this AFL cohort. A football lineman, for instance, may rarely or never reach a comparable sprint-zone speed in a game at all, which would make an imported absolute threshold meaningless for that position without being re-checked against Baylor's own data first.

**Example** — See [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]] session 4: the athlete gained confidence running in the brace and accumulated HSR via a mix of 100 m repeats and three-minute intervals, overshooting the plan - flagged by Harries as low-risk precisely because the threshold crossed was such a low %MV for that athlete.

**Related** — [[principle--percent-of-game-value-as-volume-metric]]

# A Four-Step Recipe for Building Your Own On-Field Rehab Framework

**What it is** — Harries closes the course with an explicit recipe for building a local on-field rehab framework, independent of his own specific numbers (~01:28-03:10):
1. **Split rehab into levels** - however many suits the environment (he used five; "if you want two, if you want three, if you want seven, that's up to you").
2. **Identify your pillars** - his three were submaximal/maximal velocity running, multidirectional speed and agility, and sport-specific skills; he explicitly invites extending or subdividing this list.
3. **Decide your intensity factors** - the levers used to raise or lower intensity and complexity of drills within each level/pillar (see [[framework--eight-intensity-levers-mdsa]]).
4. **Decide which exercises/drills** fit into each level, pillar and intensity-factor combination.

He closes with an explicit disclaimer: "there is very rarely a right way or a wrong way to do things in rehab... it is just one perspective... find what works for you and your environment," restating that the two equally important objectives throughout are progressing intensity and progressing complexity of sport-relevant locomotor activity.

**Why it works** — This is a template-of-a-template: rather than prescribing Harries' own five levels and three pillars as fixed, it gives the four design decisions that produced them, so a practitioner in a different sport can rebuild an equivalent framework suited to that sport's own demands.

**When to apply** — Use this exact four-step sequence as the design process for a Baylor-football-specific on-field rehab framework: keep Harries' levels/intensity-lever logic, but explicitly add the missing fourth pillar (contact/collision, per [[framework--invasion-sport-locomotor-pillars]]) at step 2, and build a football-specific drill menu at step 4 rather than reusing his AFL drill catalogue directly.

**When NOT to apply** — This recipe describes how to *build* a framework's structure; it says nothing about the specific thresholds, force benchmarks or exit criteria a framework needs to be safe (that layer is [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]] and [[heuristic--two-exposures-above-90-percent-mv-exit-rule]]). Building the four steps is necessary but not sufficient for a clinically defensible RTP process.

**Example** — Applied Performance's own review of this course already used exactly this four-step logic to plan next work: keep Harries' five levels and eight-lever table, add a football-specific contact pillar with its own dials (opponent size/intent, stance/start, hand-fighting, live vs. thud), and build a drill menu on the resulting intensity x complexity matrix by position group.

**Related** — [[framework--invasion-sport-locomotor-pillars]]; [[framework--eight-intensity-levers-mdsa]]

# A Four-Step Recipe for Building Your Own On-Field Rehab Framework

**What it is** — Harries closes the course with an explicit recipe for building a local on-field rehab framework, independent of his own specific numbers (~01:28-03:10):
1. **Split rehab into levels** - however many suits the environment (he used five; "if you want two, if you want three, if you want seven, that's up to you").
2. **Identify your pillars** - his three were submaximal/maximal velocity running, multidirectional speed and agility, and sport-specific skills; he explicitly invites extending or subdividing this list.
3. **Decide your intensity factors** - the levers used to raise or lower intensity and complexity of drills within each level/pillar (see [[framework--eight-intensity-levers-mdsa]]).
4. **Decide which exercises/drills** fit into each level, pillar and intensity-factor combination.

He closes with an explicit disclaimer: "there is very rarely a right way or a wrong way to do things in rehab... it is just one perspective... find what works for you and your environment," restating that the two equally important objectives throughout are progressing intensity and progressing complexity of sport-relevant locomotor activity.

**Why it works** — This is a template-of-a-template: rather than prescribing Harries' own five levels and three pillars as fixed, it gives the four design decisions that produced them, so a practitioner in a different sport can rebuild an equivalent framework suited to that sport's own demands.

**When to apply** — Use this exact four-step sequence as the design process for a Baylor-football-specific on-field rehab framework: keep Harries' levels/intensity-lever logic, but explicitly add the missing fourth pillar (contact/collision, per [[framework--invasion-sport-locomotor-pillars]]) at step 2, and build a football-specific drill menu at step 4 rather than reusing his AFL drill catalogue directly.

**When NOT to apply** — This recipe describes how to *build* a framework's structure; it says nothing about the specific thresholds, force benchmarks or exit criteria a framework needs to be safe (that layer is [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]] and [[heuristic--two-exposures-above-90-percent-mv-exit-rule]]). Building the four steps is necessary but not sufficient for a clinically defensible RTP process.

# AGENTS.md

Project: Flint

## What this is
Flint is Claude working as Eric's sport-science, performance, S&C and rehab thought
partner. This repo builds the knowledge base behind that role. It catalogs Eric's
Drive (his own material, TB's Training Info, Landon Evans, courses, papers), routes the
high-value sources into Zotero and the SecondBrain vault, and writes per-discipline
synthesis notes that compare the sources against Eric's own method. It is a side-lane
project, outside the prioritization-slate cap. See `README.md` for the approach and
`docs/PLAN.md` for the checklist.

## Session routine
- Start: run `git pull`, then read docs/STATUS.md before doing anything else.
- End: update docs/STATUS.md (done, next, open questions), commit, and `git push`.
- Never leave uncommitted work at the end of a session.

## Conventions
- Durable notes and decisions go in docs/, committed. Not in chat, not in cloud project docs.
- Documents, data exports, and deliverables live on the primary storage drive (Google Drive 00_Primary_Storage_Drive), not in the repo. Files over 95 MB never go in git.
- `data/` is gitignored except aggregate summaries. Regenerate the file-level manifest with `pwsh scripts/build_manifest.ps1`.
- Codex workers read staged copies in `staging/`, never the Drive root. DexaProject, athlete snapshots, Catapult and PFF exports are never catalogued.
- Books go through the ingest review gate (automated check plus an independent falsifying review) before atomization.
- Writing: plain, direct, no em dashes. Documents use the Baylor design system.
